text: The entire project expanded the school to approximately . The "new" building dedication ceremonies were held in the fall of 2000. As part of the remodeling, every classroom was wired and equipped for voice, video, and data. Each morning the student-run news show, "NewsCenter," is broadcast with the daily announcements and news. Other major construction milestones: in 1969 a swimming pool; in 1982 an additional gym, called the "New Gym" or "East Gym"; in 1995 the fieldhouse at Rice Field was doubled in size along with the re-crowning/sodding of the football playing field. The Ronzone track was resurfaced in 1995 and improved again in 2010. In the fall of 2020, the Elkhart Central name was retired, and for one year the Elkhart Central building housed Elkhart High School, East Campus. The athletics programs of the former Elkhart Central High School and Elkhart Memorial High School merged into one, with a new mascot (Lions), school colors (blue and gold), and new fight song. In the fall of 2021, the system underwent a change where students in grades 10 through 12 will attend classes on California Road at the former Elkhart Memorial (west campus)and Elkhart Area Career Center buildings, with the addition of new music rehearsal space and a new building to house technology programs. Elkhart High School was divided into six Schools of Study to better prepare students for post-high school careers. Students in grade 9 attend classes at the former Elkhart Central High School (east campus, known as the Freshman Division) on Blazer Boulevard. Demographics The demographic breakdown of the 1,641 students enrolled in 2019-2020 was: Asian - 0.7% Black - 12.2% Hispanic - 41.4% White - 38.5% Multiracial - 7.2% 59.2% of the students were eligible for free or reduced-cost lunch. For 2019–2020, Elkhart Central was a Title I school. Notable alumni Lindsay Benko – gold medalist Olympic swimmer Jean Hagen – Academy Award and Emmy Award-nominated actress David Heath – probabilist who became world-famous for developing Heath–Jarrow–Morton framework to model evolution of interest rate curve Curtis Hill – 43rd Attorney General of Indiana Ben Larson – college basketball player Alec Purdie – midfielder for MLS's New England Revolution Nathan Palmer – wide receiver for the NFL's Chicago Bears Clare Randolph – center for the NFL's Chicago Cardinals & Detroit Lions Dave Schnell – quarterback for the Indiana Hoosiers Shafer Suggs – former NFL player with the New York Jets Tanner Tully - Major League Baseball pitcher Rich Wingo – former NFL player with the Green Bay Packers Athletics Elkhart Central was a member of the Northern Indiana Conference and competed as a class 4A school, except in football where they competed in class 5A. The school’s academic offerings reflect a commitment to diverse educational paths, emphasizing both traditional coursework and vocational training. The restructuring into Schools of Study encourages interdisciplinary learning, allowing students to tailor their educational experience toward specific professional interests. These schools include disciplines such as STEM, humanities, arts, and career and technical education, providing pathways that align with contemporary workforce demands. The integration of technology into the curriculum is evident across all grade levels, facilitated by the infrastructure upgrades completed in the early 2000s. Athletic competition remains a central component of the school experience, with the program maintaining a high level of competitive engagement within its conference structure. The athletic facilities have been continually upgraded to support the growing demands of the student body and the quality of the athletic programs. The merger of the athletic departments created a unified program that aimed to leverage the strengths of both predecessor schools while establishing a new institutional identity. The dedication to community involvement extends beyond the athletic field, with various clubs and service learning opportunities available to students. These extracurricular activities complement the academic rigor and contribute to the holistic development of the student population. Furthermore, the school district has invested in ongoing professional development for its teaching staff, ensuring that educators remain current with pedagogical advancements and subject matter changes. The transition periods, such as the temporary housing of the East Campus, presented logistical challenges but ultimately spurred improvements in facility utilization and operational efficiency across the campus footprint.

Life and career Weygand was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts, to Charles E. Weygand and Lillian M. (Kingsley) Weygand. Raphael Academy for his high school years, attended the University of Rhode Island where he became a member of Theta Chi Fraternity. He received a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Theater in 1971, a Bachelor of Science in Civil and Environmental Engineering in 1976, a Master of Arts in Political Science in 2009 and a Masters of Public Administration in 2010 all from the University of Rhode Island. A landscape architect for the Rhode Island Department of Natural Resources from 1973 to 1977, a city planner and landscape architect for an architectural firm from 1977 to 1982, he founded and was president of Weygand, Orchich, & Christie, Inc., an architectural and landscape architectural firm from 1982 to 1993. He was elected a Fellow of the American Society of Landscape Architects in 1998. In 1991, Weygand, then a state legislator, was offered a $2,000 bribe by then-Pawtucket Mayor Brian J. Weygand went to the Rhode Island State Police and the FBI and agreed to deal with the mayor and provide evidence of the bribe. Wearing the listening equipment, Weygand met with Sarault in the mayor's office. After Weygand left, FBI agents burst in and arrested the mayor. The evidence Weygand provided helped send the mayor, several other city officials and private vendors to prison. Weygand served as chairman of the East Providence Planning Board from 1978 to 1984, a member of the Rhode Island House of Representatives from 1985 to 1993, and as the 65th Lieutenant Governor of Rhode Island from 1993 to 1997. In 1996, he was elected to an open seat in Congress that was being vacated by incoming Senator Jack Reed. Weygand did not seek re-election to the United States House of Representatives in 2000, opting to challenge Republican Senator Lincoln Chafee. Weygand, an anti-abortion Democrat, lost the election to Chafee, who enjoyed popularity among Rhode Island Democrats as one of the most liberal Republicans elected to national office. In 2001, Weygand was appointed President of the New England Board of Higher Education in Boston. In 2004, he stepped down at NEBHE to take a new position as Vice President for Administration at the University of Rhode Island. In 2013, Weygand stepped down from the administration to take a faculty position as the director of the University of Rhode Island MPA program. His tenure at the University of Rhode Island saw him contribute significantly to the public administration curriculum, focusing on governance and regional development within New England. The transition from legislative and executive roles to academia marked a shift toward concentrating his expertise on policy analysis and educational leadership. His involvement with the MPA program reflected a continued dedication to shaping future public servants capable of navigating complex municipal and state challenges. The breadth of his professional experience, spanning private practice, state government, and higher education administration, provided a unique perspective to his academic endeavors. He often lectured on the intersection of urban planning, political maneuvering, and environmental stewardship, drawing directly from his years working with the Department of Natural Resources and as a city planner. These diverse engagements allowed him to develop a comprehensive understanding of how policy is formulated, implemented, and often compromised within a democratic structure. His service in Congress, though brief, provided firsthand insight into the national political machinery and the challenges of representing a district with varied economic and social concerns. The ethical dilemma surrounding the Pawtucket mayoral bribery case remains a notable aspect of his public service record, illustrating his willingness to employ legal and investigative means to combat corruption. This willingness to engage in difficult political battles contrasted with his later, more contemplative role in university administration. Throughout his career, a consistent thread has been a deep concern for the sustainable development of Rhode Island, whether through green infrastructure planning or sound fiscal policy. His involvement with professional organizations further cemented his status as an influential figure within the regional planning and governmental spheres. The cumulative effect of his varied professional life suggests a dedication not merely to a specific field, but to the holistic improvement of the community and the institutions that govern it.

These species descriptions reflect the complex taxonomic history of the genus Enoplognatha, a group of spiders known for their diverse morphology and often cryptic habits. The consistent reassignments and synonymizations highlight the challenges inherent in classifying arthropods, particularly when specimens are collected from disparate geographical locations or when initial morphological assessments lack the requisite fine detail for modern phylogenetic analysis. Many of the historical names, such as those attributed to Koch or Fickert, have been integrated into broader, more encompassing taxa as subsequent research has refined our understanding of interspecific variation within the genus. For example, the grouping around Enoplognatha caricis appears frequently, suggesting it may represent a morphologically adaptable or highly variable lineage within the spider's evolutionary tree. The inclusion of type locality information, such as "T from Steatoda" or "T from Theridion," provides crucial historical context regarding the initial identification and the taxonomic confusion that arose when these spiders were sometimes misidentified as members of other spider families. More recent studies employing molecular techniques have played a vital role in clarifying these relationships, often confirming or overturning the classifications established in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Some of the names retained, such as Enoplognatha joshua Chamberlin & Ivie, suggest specific biogeographic or morphological characteristics were deemed sufficiently unique to warrant independent species status, despite overlapping characteristics with other established taxa. The genus Enoplognatha itself is recognized for its relatively slender build and the specific arrangement of its chelicerae, features that have been key diagnostic traits throughout arachnological literature. Furthermore, ecological preferences, ranging from terrestrial environments to those associated with specific vegetation types, provide valuable ancillary data when attempting to delineate species boundaries, although these factors alone are rarely sufficient for formal taxonomic delineation. The ongoing revision of spider taxonomy continues to be an active area of biological research, driven by both the discovery of undescribed diversity and the application of advanced systematic methodologies.

These scholarly works represent diverse approaches to interpreting the legal and narrative elements found within the books of the Torah, particularly focusing on passages like Deuteronomy. Some analyses employ deep dives into the sociopolitical implications of biblical law, examining how ancient Israel structured its communal governance and judicial systems. Others take a more rhetorical or literary approach, investigating the narrative techniques employed by the biblical authors to convey ethical imperatives. The study of cities of refuge, for instance, has drawn attention from both legal scholars and those interested in covenantal relationships, exploring the balance between divine ordinance and human compassion within the framework of early Israelite society. Modern commentaries often seek to bridge the gap between the ancient text and contemporary ethical concerns, translating archaic legal codes into relevant moral frameworks for modern readers. Furthermore, some research integrates archaeological findings with biblical textual analysis, offering tangible context to the lived experiences of ordinary individuals within the ancient landscape described in the Torah. The varying methodologies employed across these texts—from strict textual criticism to historical-critical analysis and gendered readings—reflect the breadth of contemporary biblical scholarship regarding the enduring questions posed by the foundational scriptures.

Juha Malinen (born 16 July 1958) is a Finnish football coach with a total of 20 seasons at the highest level. Malinen manages Veikkausliiga club KTP. Managerial career Malinen was born in Oulu. He was coming to the end of his short career as a football player in 1978 when he decided to enroll as a student at the University of Oulu Department of Education. He started his career as a teacher just before he would have graduated, and thus didn't complete his studies. While working as a teacher he found himself yearning for a job where he could see more concretely the impact of his work. He soon became interested in football coaching. In 1986 Malinen found a job at Kastelli Sports Gymnasium (secondary education) as the school's football coach. Among his students at Kastelli were Antti Niemi and Mika Nurmela who went on to become Finnish internationals. Ville Nylund and Aarno Turpeinen, who later became core players of top team in Finland, HJK Helsinki, were also at Kastelli. Besides coaching at Kastelli, Malinen taught sports and crafts at a nearby school for hearing-impaired persons. The Kastelli football team was unexpectedly successful in 1989 when it qualified for the School World Championships 1989, held in Florence, Italy. Malinen's "brickwall" -tactic was a good match with inexperienced Finns, which didn't lose any games, but were still knocked out in second stage by France (Auxerre academy) with penalties. France became the champions and Kastelli finished in 5th place. It was this tournament, where Malinen first gained reputation and proved to himself that he could lead a successful career as a football manager. After Kastelli, Malinen was hired as a manager of Rauman Pallo. During his time at Rauma, he became full-time football manager. Two players from Kastelli, Antti Niemi and Mika Nurmela followed Malinen to Rauman Pallo. U15 and U16 national teams In summer 1990 Malinen was made U15 and U16 national team manager by Finnish FA. He led his team in 1991 and 1992 European Championships. After about four years of coaching the national teams Malinen wanted to get back into more rapid life of club football. Shows promise in Premier League He returned to his hometown Oulu and FC Oulu, which did get promoted next year. His tenure at FC Oulu marked a significant turning point in his managerial progression. He guided the club through the challenging environment of the Veikkausliiga, building a foundation for future success. The club's ascent in the league structure provided Malinen with the platform to demonstrate his tactical acumen and leadership capabilities on a higher competitive stage. His coaching philosophy, which prioritized defensive solidity combined with disciplined attacking structures, began to gain recognition within Finnish football circles. The success at FC Oulu naturally drew attention from clubs operating in stronger leagues, notably those in the English Premier League. An opportunity arose that allowed Malinen to test his skills against elite European competition, a move many viewed as a significant career elevation. While the stint in England proved challenging in terms of immediate results, the experience provided invaluable exposure to the rigorous demands and high standards of top-tier European football. Upon returning to Finland, his reputation had grown considerably, positioning him as one of the country's more experienced and sought-after coaches. His subsequent appointments reflected this elevated status, leading to sustained involvement with prominent Veikkausliiga sides. His ability to mentor younger talent and instill a professional ethos became a hallmark of his coaching style. The consistent demand for his expertise solidified his status as a respected figure within the domestic coaching community, even as he explored varied tactical approaches across different teams.

Grant sings several of the songs, which made Night and Day the closest he came to making a musical after the end of his stage career. He was described by his biographer as a "competent though not a very expressive singer." Production of the film was impeded by a 1945 strike of the Conference of Studio Workers, who represented film set builders. Reception In a review upon release of the film, Thomas Pyror of The New York Times called the film "a generally pleasant and musically exciting show." The Times praised the musical numbers and the performances by Grant and Woolley, but noted the straying from historical fact and the thin and conventional scenario the scenarists concocted about the fabulous Mr. Porter." In 2004, at the debut of another film on Porter's life, De-Lovely, the Times called Night and Day "so-bad-it's-almost-good." The newspaper recounted that when Night and Day was being filmed, "Orson Welles cracked: 'What will they use for a climax? The only suspense is: will he or won't he accumulate $10 million?'" The soundtrack for the film features a variety of musical styles, ranging from upbeat jazz numbers to more sentimental ballads, reflecting the diverse social milieu of the characters depicted. While the musical sequences were a critical component of the film's appeal, the integration of the songs into the narrative was often considered disjointed by critics. The presence of various guest singers and dancers highlights the studio's effort to create a lavish and entertaining picture, characteristic of the musical comedies popular during that era. Many of the featured songs were either original compositions for the film or standards from the Great American Songbook, allowing the production to tap into existing popular musical tastes of the time. The inclusion of authentic musical talent, such as Mary Martin portraying her real-life counterpart, added a layer of meta-commentary to the picture regarding the performing arts. The film's visual presentation, replete with elaborate dance sequences and colorful set designs, aimed to provide a spectacle commensurate with the escapist nature of its premise. Despite the uneven quality of the screenplay, the visual grandeur and the enduring popularity of some of the featured musical moments ensured that Night and Day maintained a certain cultural footprint in cinematic history.

He was listed as twenty-three years old in 1887 when approximately 800 Tsimshians from "Old Metlakatla," B.C., founded the community of "New Metlakatla," Alaska. He was a member of the Gispwudwada (Killerwhale clan) of the Tsimshian and was raised by an uncle and aunt, Henry and Alice Ridley. He was also related to the Rev. He was well liked by the Anglican lay minister William Duncan, founder of the Christian utopian communities at both Old and New Metlakatla. When Simpson was a young man, he was one of the eight people sent in a canoe by Duncan from New Metlakatla to dismantle the church they had left behind at Old Metlakatla. In one version of the story they hacked it to pieces and burned it to the ground and escaped back to Alaska before they could face prosecution. Not all histories of Old Metlakatla record this as the cause of the fire that destroyed the church in 1901; the story may arise from a much earlier incident. Simpson along with another Metlakatla Tsimshian, Mark Hamilton, were the principal investors in the sawmill community of Port Gravina, near Ketchikan, Alaska, from its founding in 1892 until it burned in 1904. This was an offshoot of the Metlakatla community, one committed to Presbyterianism under Marsden. After the fire, Simpson moved to Juneau, and then to Sitka where he was the owner of a boatbuilding business. In 1912, Simpson became chairman of the committee that was eventually to form the Alaska Native Brotherhood (ANB), and the committee's only non-Tlingit member. He is considered the father of the ANB and also "the father of Land Claims" in Alaska, the long process that led to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (without Metlakatla's participation), long after his death. Simpson is widely known for his famous quotation, uttered to the Tlingit land-claims activist William Paul at the 1925 ANB convention: "Willie, who owns this land?" William Paul (after a long pause): "We do." Peter Simpson: "Then fight for it." One biography of Paul, Then Fight for It, by Fred Paul (William's son), derives its title from this exchange. His influence extended beyond the formal structures of early Native political organizing; he was a central figure in the cultural and social life of the Metlakatla people during a period of intense external pressure and assimilationist policies. Simpson maintained a complex relationship with the various religious influences present in the communities, balancing the Christian teachings introduced by Duncan with traditional Tsimshian cultural practices. His involvement in the sawmill venture at Port Gravina demonstrates an early engagement with economic enterprise outside the strictly communal models prevalent in the Metlakatla settlements. This venture represented an attempt by a segment of the community to participate in the burgeoning resource extraction economy of Southeast Alaska. The eventual failure of the Port Gravina enterprise further mirrored the economic precariousness facing many indigenous groups in the region as external markets and governmental regulations shifted. His leadership role in the nascent Alaska Native Brotherhood was pivotal, as the ANB sought to provide a unified front for various indigenous groups facing common challenges regarding land rights and cultural preservation. The inclusion of non-Tlingit members on the early committees, while perhaps not always representative of the broader spectrum of indigenous opinion, indicated a growing recognition of the need for broader strategic alliances to navigate the complex legal and political landscape of the Territory of Alaska. Simpson's famous challenge to William Paul crystallized the core philosophical divide of the era: whether indigenous sovereignty was a matter of inherent right or a legal entitlement to be aggressively defended against encroaching external claims. This articulation became a rallying cry for subsequent generations of Alaskan Natives advocating for self-determination and the recognition of ancestral tenure.

His extensive portfolio demonstrates a sustained engagement with significant civic, corporate, and cultural architecture across various governmental and private sectors. The firm's involvement in projects such as the expansion of the Dulles Airport terminal highlights its capacity to handle large-scale infrastructural demands while maintaining aesthetic rigor. Furthermore, the transformation of existing structures, exemplified by the renovation of Lever House, showcases a commitment to adaptive reuse within the high-density urban environment. The continuous evolution of the News & World Report headquarters itself reflects the firm's ability to meet the changing operational needs of major media organizations while maintaining a distinct architectural presence. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill’s work in Washington, D.C., frequently intersects with governmental planning and public space design, necessitating a high degree of sensitivity to established urban precedents and regulatory frameworks. The selection of sites and the execution of designs for prominent hotels, such as the Four Seasons and Park Hyatt Washington, underscores the firm's proficiency in the luxury hospitality sector, where design must seamlessly blend functional efficiency with elevated user experience. The deliberate choice to anchor major corporate and media presences within architecturally significant structures, such as the Time Warner Center and the various properties at 450 Lexington Avenue, positions the firm at the forefront of modern metropolitan development trends. The inclusion of international projects, like the Embassy of the United States in Ottawa, broadens the scope of the firm’s expertise beyond the American context, requiring adherence to diverse international standards for diplomatic and high-profile institutional building. These varied commissions reveal a versatile practice capable of addressing challenges ranging from monumental public works to highly detailed commercial interiors. The ongoing development and evolution of the firm's principal office locations in Manhattan also serve as a barometer for contemporary architectural design philosophy in the financial and media hubs of the world.

While most early conservationists, with few exceptions, implicated themselves in the apartheid system, groups such as Earthlife Africa were consciously aware of their role as nurturers of freedom and human rights as well as the rights of the earth and animal kingdom. The Cape Town Ecology Group for example, openly campaigned for political freedoms with a platform that "ecologised politics and politicised ecology". During apartheid while political parties were banned, environmental groups served as an outlet for activism and political expression. In Durban, the Environmental Justice Network, sprung up alongside ant-apartheid issues that affected the environment as well as the rights of workers. While many radical environmentalists were later absorbed into the governing African National Congress, some toyed with the formation of a political party that would represent green interests. The environmental movement moved into the political space in 1989 with the establishment of the Ecology Party, which disbanded shortly thereafter. In 1992 Ian Brownlie launched the Green Party, but it too disbanded after a disastrous election campaign in 1994. Judy Sole then founded the Government of the People Green Party in 1999. Timeline Colonial Era 1918: Native Farmers Association founded; 1926: Wildlife Society of South Africa founded Apartheid Era 1955: Congress_of_the_People_(1955) held at Kliptown. Freedom Charter includes article on agrarian & environmental rights, in particular 'save the soil'. 1973: Endangered Wildlife Trust founded 1976 Koeberg Alert founded following the decision to site South Africa's first nuclear power station only 30 kms from Cape Town 1977: The Dolphin Action & Protection Group founded with the motto and policy 'Dolphins Should Be Free'. 1983: Koeberg Alert reconstituted, "broadens the focus of the protest" to place the entire nuclear issue "within its social, political and economic context." 1984: Natsoc, a nature society founded 1986: Chernobyl disaster 1987: Cape Town Ecology Group founded; with motto: 'Free the Humans' 1988: Earthlife Africa formed; Khanyisa, environmental awareness organisation founded in townships of Langa, Nyanga, Guguletu and Khayelitsha 1989: Earthlife Africa exposes mercury poisoning of workers at Thor Chemicals; Kagenna Magazine is published; Green Action Forum founded by Greg Knill. Establishment of the Ecology Party in Cape Town. 1990: A fishing industry campaign by the Food and Allied Workers Union links workers issues to the environment. 1991: First National Conference on Environment and Development; Environmental Monitoring Group releases a document "Towards Sustainable Development in South Africa"; General Magnus Malan takes over as new Minister of Water Affairs and Forestry; Bev Geach of the Weekly Mail publishes The Green Pages, a directory of environmental groups 1992: Earthlife Africa pressurizes the government for an inquiry into asbestos related deaths. These activities illustrate the deep entanglement of environmental concern with broader social justice movements during the period of institutionalized racial segregation. The direct linkage between ecological degradation and the well-being of marginalized communities became a defining characteristic of environmental advocacy in South Africa. Campaigns against industrial pollution, for instance, frequently overlapped with struggles for labor rights and basic human dignity, demonstrating that environmentalism was not a purely scientific or aesthetic concern but a socio-political imperative. The emergence of groups operating within townships reflected a grassroots understanding that environmental health and human rights were inextricably linked, often providing the first organized platform for residents to challenge systemic injustices perpetuated by both the state and industrial entities. This confluence of concerns laid the groundwork for a more holistic understanding of sustainability that transcended traditional disciplinary boundaries. As the political climate began to shift toward democratic transition in the late 1980s and early 1990s, these environmental activist networks possessed a unique institutional memory and a history of non-violent direct action, providing crucial experiential capital for the emerging democratic structures. The pressure exerted by these well-organized, often locally rooted groups contributed significantly to the national dialogue surrounding resource management, development planning, and accountability during the complex transition to a non-racial democracy. Their early work established precedents for public participation in decision-making processes regarding land use and industrial siting, setting a standard for environmental governance in the post-apartheid era.

Lieutenant-Colonel Thomas Higginson (January 9, 1794 – January 22, 1884) was an Irish-born soldier, civic official and politician in Ontario, Canada. Overview The son of Boyd Higginson and Jane Crawford, he was born in County Antrim and came to Canada in 1819 with his three older brothers, settling in Hawkesbury. In the same year, before leaving Ireland, he had married Nancy Agnes Park. Thomas Higginson contributed to social, educational and spiritual development of Vankleek Hill, Ontario and district during the early stages of community formation. He was the second postmaster of Vankleek Hill; the first was Neil Stewart who served when the post office was established in 1827. Neil Stewart and Thomas Higginson were the first to represent the district of West Hawkesbury c. 1844 on the newly established district council. He was Superintendent of Schools for Prescott and Russell for many years, an Agent for the Bank of Upper Canada for the transmission of the proceeds of sales of public lands, and a member of the County Council. Lieutenant-Colonel Higginson was founder of the Mechanics' Institute in Vankleek Hill in 1857 and its first president. According to diary entries by Thomas Tweed Higginson, for March 30, 1859, “Uncle Thomas preparing a lecture to be delivered before the Mechanic’s Institute: ‘The Change of the Earth’s Surface’.” In 1856 St. John’s Anglican Church was completed on land owned by Lieutenant-Colonel Thomas Higginson. Before this, Lieutenant-Colonel Higginson was involved in establishing a Sunday School that served Vankleek Hill. The first issue of the weekly news publication The Economist in Vankleek Hill in 1858 was edited by Rupert Mearse Wells (later Speaker of the Provincial Legislature) and contained articles and poetry by Lieutenant-Colonel Higginson. The Higginson Tower The Higginson Tower is close to St. John the Apostle Anglican Church (the church on the hill along Highway 34 as you enter Vankleek Hill from the north end). The ruins were once near the home of Lieutenant-Colonel Thomas Higginson, who built it in 1832. William Higginson, Thomas' son, added the upper portion to create a conservatory and also built the red brick house nearby. His construction of this edifice reflected his interest in both utility and aesthetic permanence within the developing landscape of the township. The tower itself served as a distinctive local landmark, speaking to the aspirations of the early settlers who sought to establish enduring symbols of their community's growth and stability. Alongside his private endeavors, Higginson maintained a consistent involvement in the political and administrative life of the region. His tenure on various municipal bodies provided him with a platform to influence local policy and infrastructure development, particularly concerning education and public services. These roles required considerable administrative acumen and a commitment to the practical needs of a growing agricultural and nascent industrial community. His efforts were part of a broader provincial trend during the mid-nineteenth century where local figures took proactive roles in shaping the social fabric outside of major urban centres. The establishment of institutions such as the Mechanics' Institute underscored a belief in the power of self-improvement and practical learning among the populace. These institutes provided spaces for learned discourse, technical instruction, and cultural exchange, mirroring broader societal movements across British North America. His dedication to these varied pursuits—from civil service to religious patronage and educational reform—demonstrates a multifaceted commitment to the progress of Vankleek Hill during its formative decades. The legacy of his actions is embedded in the institutional framework and the physical landmarks that characterize the area today.

Salamat Dar Al Messiria in Darfur, Sudan The area known as Nitega (نتيقة) is the mainland of the Messiria in Dar Fur, among the landmarks in the area is the Mountain Karou (جبل كرو). Second Sudanese Civil War: 1983–2005 Background of the conflict The Misseriyya mostly live around Kordofan and migrate south into the Dinka territory. They are marginally represented in Darfur and there they live a semi-sedentary life. The Misseriyya was once a larger group, but fragmented into smaller groups over time. The location of Messiria of Kordofan is at the border zone between Sudan and Southern Sudan, specially the southern Fringes of their nomadic zone. The Abyei area is claimed by Messira as well as by Ngok Dinka, to be theirs. While the Messiria are Baggara Arabs, Sunni Muslims and identified as Northerners, on the other hand, Ngok Dinka are Southerners and identified as Africans either Christians or Animists. Henderson, MacMichael and Ian Cunnison all attest the presence of Messiria in the eighteenth century. Similar history is also available for the nine Ngok Dinka chiefdoms on the same area. Being both nomads, The Messiria and Dinka coexisted for long time and shared the grazing resources. Those Messiria who have most contact with Ngok Dinka are the Messiria Humr. The Messiria Zurug share most of their land with the Nuba tribes, along the western sides of the national highway connecting Deling city to Kadugli; the capital city of South Kordofan and extending to Talodi city. On the eastern side of this national highway found the Hawazma tribes sharing the land also with the Nuba tribes. The Nuba are indigenous Africans inhabiting the area known as Nuba Mountains of Southern Kordofan and mostly Sunni Muslims. Both Nuba and Dinka are sided with Southern Rebels (SPLA/SPLM) during the civil war, while Messiria and Hawazma sided with Sudanese Government. Historical grazing disputes During the dry season the Misseriya migrate to the river Kiir in Abyei. They call the region the Bahr Al Arab. Both branches of Messiria, the Humr and the Zurug, are involved in historical grazing disputes and isolated fights along their southern borders, either with Dinka, Nuer or Nuba over grazing and water resources. The traditional fighting was intensified during the first Southern guerrilla's fighting, called Anyanya, in 1964 when a whole Messiria nomad camp around lake Abyyad was massacred in a terrible human slaughter by Anyanya fighters, none were spared including children, elderly and brides; many Messiria were abducted and women were raped by the rebels. This atrocity marked a significant escalation of the tensions between the nomadic groups and the emerging southern resistance forces. Following this event, the relationship between the Messiria and the Dinka peoples became increasingly adversarial, moving beyond mere resource competition into deep-seated ethnic and political animosity. The protracted nature of the civil conflict saw these localized disputes become embedded within the broader narrative of Sudanese conflict. The differing affiliations during the Second Sudanese Civil War hardened these lines of demarcation, with tribal loyalties often aligning with the political factions supporting the government or the southern liberation movements. The cultural and historical interactions that once fostered coexistence fractured under the pressures of ideological conflict and political mobilization. Furthermore, the economic necessity of transhumance, which dictated the seasonal movements of the Messiria flocks and herds, placed them in direct, inevitable contact with settled or semi-sedentary populations, magnifying the potential for conflict over arable land and water points. The varying religious affiliations, while not always the primary driver of conflict, provided additional layers of identity that were exploited by political actors in the regional power struggles. Efforts toward peace and reconciliation have frequently been hampered by the unresolved issues pertaining to land rights, historical grievances, and the security of nomadic routes, issues that remain central to the political landscape of the region even after the formal end of the civil war.

Career Charles had an exceptionally long acting career that spanned over seven decades. She made her stage debut as the Dormouse in a 1945 production of Alice in Wonderland at the Connaught Theatre, Worthing and her West End theatre debut in the Pick up Girl at the Prince of Wales Theatre in 1946. Charles appeared in the original London production of The Boy Friend as 'Dulcie' which ran for a total of 2,082 performances (from 1954 to 1959). She played the part of 'Solange Lafitte' in the original West End production of Follies at the Shaftesbury Theatre by Stephen Sondheim. The show ran for 644 performances from 21 July 1987 to 4 February 1989 and starred Julia McKenzie, Daniel Massey and Eartha Kitt. Charles has worked extensively in theatre, TV and films and has carved a niche for herself on television playing clingy Jewish mothers. She appeared in the memorable BBC Play for Today anthology TV series (which ran from 1970 to 1984), in the TV play the Bar Mitzvah Boy which won the BAFTA, British Academy Television Award for (best single play); in 1977 it was placed 56th in a BFI poll of the 100 Greatest British Television Programmes of the 20th century, voted by industry professionals. She also played Maureen Lipman's character's mother in the ITV sitcom Agony from 1979 to 1981. In 1981 she starred in Nell Dunn's new comedy play, Steaming at the Comedy Theatre Stratford East, playing alongside Brenda Blethyn; the production won the Laurence Olivier Award for Best New Comedy that year. Other notable television credits included well known television series such as Z-Cars, Crossroads, Secret Army, Brideshead Revisited, Coronation Street, Whoops Apocalypse, Boon, Never the Twain, Lovejoy, Casualty, Holby City and Bad Girls. Her notable film credits included: Sisterhood, Hot Fuzz, Cuba, Revenge of the Pink Panther, Victor Victoria, and Sixty Six. Personal life and death Charles died on 21 April 2023, at the age of 93. She was survived by two daughters; Kelly, an actress, and Samantha, a production stage manager. Stage appearances (Stage debut) Dormouse, Alice in Wonderland, Connaught Theatre, Worthing, England, 1945 (London West End debut) Ruby Lockwood, The Pick-Up Girl, Prince of Wales Theatre, London, 1946 Rosie, Women of Twilight, Vaudeville Theatre, London, 1951 See You Again (Sandy Wilson revue), Watergate Theatre, London, 1952 Swing Back the Gate (Geoffrey Wright, revue), Irving Theatre, London, 1952. Her acting range allowed her to move seamlessly between light comedy and more dramatic roles throughout her extensive career. The specific typecasting in the role of the maternal figure became a recognizable aspect of her screen persona, a character type that she inhabited with a particular blend of warmth and exasperation. While theatre remained a significant part of her professional life, her television presence cemented her place in the public consciousness for a generation of British viewers. Her work in film, though perhaps less numerous than her television appearances, showcased her ability to adapt her stagecraft to the demands of the cinematic medium. The diversity of her filmography suggests a willingness to engage with various genres, from action-comedy to more character-driven pieces. The longevity of her career is a testament to her adaptability, her commitment to her craft, and her ability to maintain relevance across changing entertainment landscapes. Later in her career, she continued to take on roles that reflected both her established strengths and her desire for new challenges. The transition from the golden age of British television to the modern era saw her continuing to contribute to the arts in various capacities.

It appears to implicate the king as the divine lord of his own day. Inversely, at San Bartolo, the divine hero of the day 'King', Hunahpu, substitutes for the real king. Setting up a stela may additionally have involved the notion of the king as a protective 'tree of life'. Moreover, in the Classic period, the king is commonly depicted holding a cosmic serpent from whose jaws deities (often those of rain, lightning and fire) emerge; the king's raising and balancing of this serpent, accompanied by his 'conjuring' of the emerging deities, may well have been expressed and supported by ritual. Ancestor worship During the Classic period, Tikal's North Acropolis consisted of nucleated royal burial temples and is even referred to as a 'necropolis'. In Classic-period royal courts, tombs are generally found integrated in the residences of the nobility. Apart from the ancestral remains themselves, sacred bundles left by the ancestors were also an object of veneration. Reliefs from the Classic-period kingdom of Yaxchilan also show that royal ancestors were sometimes approached during bloodletting rituals and then appeared to their descendants, emerging from the mouth of a terrestrial serpent (which has been nicknamed 'Vision Serpent'). The monthly feast cycle of the Postclassic kingdom of Maní included a commemorative festival for an ancestral hero viewed as the founder of Yucatec kingship, Kukulcan (a name corresponding to Quichean Gucumatz and Aztec Quetzalcoatl). Around 1500, the incinerated remains of the (male) members of notable Yucatec families were enclosed in wooden images which, together with the 'idols', were placed on the house altar, and ritually fed on all festive occasions; alternatively, they were placed in an urn, and a temple was built over it (Landa). In the Verapaz, a statue of the dead king was placed on his burial mound, which then became a place of worship. Sciences of destiny Numerology and calendrics Apart from writing, the fundamental priestly sciences were arithmetics and calendrics. Within the social group of the priests at court, it had by Classical times become customary to deify the numbers as well as the basic day-unit, and – particularly in the south-eastern kingdoms of Copan and Quirigua – to conceive the mechanism of time as a sort of relay or estafette in which the 'burden' of the time-units was passed on from one divine numerical 'bearer' to the next one. These sophisticated temporal concepts suggest an intricate cosmological understanding wherein the passage of time was not merely a linear progression but a cyclical or tiered process governed by divine numerical entities. Astronomical observations were thus intrinsically linked to religious doctrine, providing the empirical basis for theological assertions regarding cosmic order. The precision required for agricultural planning and ritual scheduling necessitated advanced mathematical knowledge, which the ruling elite monopolized. This control over time, symbolized and mathematically codified, reinforced the perceived divine mandate of the king, who acted as the intermediary between the mortal realm and the celestial cycles. The manipulation of calendrical knowledge was therefore a potent tool of political legitimation, as the ruler's rituals were timed to coincide with auspicious celestial events. Furthermore, the observation of planetary movements, particularly Venus, held significant ritual and military importance across various Maya polities. The cycles of Venus were often integrated into the dynastic histories and the prophesied movements of ruling lineages, tying the fate of the kingdom directly to the movements of celestial bodies. These interlocking systems of astronomy, numerology, and ancestor veneration formed a complex ideological framework underpinning Maya political and social organization.

Career Throughout the war he worked for the Polish Resistance, and was taken prisoner by both the Soviets and the Nazis. His exhibitions of mostly expressionist and abstract paintings 1946-1996 included ninety solo and group exhibitions, among the latter in Germany, 1946; England, 1954, 1961; and America, 1961; as well as the Olympic Games, National Gallery of Victoria, 1956; Survey 1, NGV, 1958; 1st Helena Rubinstein Travelling Art Scholarship, Art Gallery of New South Wales, 1958; Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery, 1959; Heide Museum of Modern Art, Melbourne, 1961, 1996–1997; New Directions, Newcastle City Art Gallery, New South Wales, 1962; Critics' Choice, Contemporary Art Society, Adelaide, 1967; South Australian painters, Adelaide Festival Centre (AFC), 1974; 50 Years of SA Art, Art Gallery of South Australia (AGSA), 1978; Painting in South Australia Today, AGSA, 1981; Five Polish Artists in Adelaide, AFC, 1986; Polish-Australian Artists, AFC 1994–1995; Charles Nodrum Gallery, Melbourne, 1985, 1990; Adelaide Town Hall, 1993–94; 20th Century Style: Furniture, AGSA, 2003; and two or three person exhibitions at Royal SA Society of Arts Gallery, Adelaide, 1951; University of Adelaide, 1966; and Kensington Gallery, Adelaide 1991. On arriving in Adelaide he designed sets for several plays, then from 1956, following injuries received in a traffic accident for some years was forced to give up painting and returned to stage production. Drawing on war-time experience as a director of the Great Theatre, Lwow, and of his own theatre in DP camps in Bavaria after the war he formed the Art Studio Players in Adelaide, working with the "Method", 1959–62. He also directed two plays for the Adelaide University Theatre Guild, in 1959 and 1967, and later appeared as an actor in several television dramas for Crawford Productions in Melbourne. His subsequent directorial work encompassed a range of theatrical styles, though his early influences remained rooted in the dramatic intensity of his wartime experiences. The Art Studio Players became a significant early vehicle for his dramatic sensibilities, allowing him to experiment with ensemble work and a heightened sense of emotional realism. Following the dissolution of this initial group, his focus broadened across various independent and subsidized theatre ventures within the South Australian cultural scene. He maintained a keen interest in the intersection of visual art and performance, often incorporating abstract or highly stylized elements into his stage designs, reflecting the concerns evident in his earlier painting practice. During the late 1960s and 1970s, he began collaborating more frequently with contemporary playwrights, pushing the boundaries of traditional narrative structure. This period saw him engage with experimental theatre groups, which favored non-linear storytelling and multimedia integration, moving away from strict adherence to classical dramatic forms. His commitment to mentorship also grew, as he began offering workshops in dramatic technique and scenic design to emerging local artists. These workshops were particularly influential in developing a generation of theatre practitioners who valued cross-disciplinary artistic dialogue. His transition from primary director to a more multifaceted creative consultant allowed him to participate in larger, more ambitious productions, both in Adelaide and in touring companies across Australia. He advised on set construction and visual concept development for several major regional theatre festivals. While his visual art output slowed considerably after the accident, his conceptual framework remained active, subtly informing the spatial dynamics and aesthetic choices of his stage productions. The technical demands of stagecraft, particularly lighting and scenography, became the primary medium through which his artistic vision was realized in the post-injury years. Later in his career, he took on roles that bridged the gap between theatre and educational institutions. He served as a guest lecturer at the University of Adelaide, discussing the socio-political context of wartime art and its subsequent translation into performance. This later phase of his career was marked by a retrospective engagement with his own body of work, both painted and performed, creating curated exhibitions that traced the trajectory of his artistic evolution from resistance fighter to stage innovator. His influence on regional Australian theatre is often cited as a prime example of how the experiences of displacement and political turmoil can catalyze a profound transformation in an artist’s chosen medium.

Norman conquest and medieval period 'Sceaplei' is mentioned in the Domesday Book, written in 1086. Shepley's population suffered during William the Conqueror's Harrying of the North 1069–1070 when the king laid to waste towns and villages between the Scottish border and the River Humber in order to put down a northern rebellion against his Norman rule. Thousands of people were put to the sword. However, the village was soon back in political favour, as in 1217, a certain Matthew of Sheplei was knighted and his name appears in the records of the Beaumont family of Whitley Beaumont and later of Bretton Hall near Wakefield. There is a reference to Shepley in the Inquisitions Post Mortem, written in the 33rd year of Henry III's reign (1249). "Extent. Scheplay alias Sepeleya town, a capital messuage, 6l. rents from free tenants, 6s. 10d. from cottars, a mill, a little wood, &c. tenure unspecified." If the township of Shepley was subinfeudated before 1166, Shepley's mesne tenancy would have been held by William de Neville, husband of Amabel, daughter of Adam, son of Sveinn. By the 13th century, the tenancy had passed to the Burgh family. Shepley Hall, situated on Station Road, was the manor house for the village. In 1361 Robert de Goldthorpe, who was also known as Robert Robertson (his father's name was Robert), married Esabell de Shepley and, as a result inherited part of the manor and estates of Shepley. In 1542, during the reign of Henry VIII (Tudor) Thomas Goldthorpe sold his share of Shepley manor and other lands for £290 to a certain Richard Stansfield and thereby appeared to terminate the family's connection with the manor. However, in the local fines records for 1543, it states "William Goldthorp, gent Manor of Shepley, also called Shepley Hall, and tenements in Shepley and Burton . 19th century In the early 19th century, Sir Joseph Radcliffe from Milnsbridge House was Lord of the Manor. He was knighted for his role in suppressing the Luddites in the Huddersfield area following the murder of Marsden mill owner William Horsfall in 1812. In 1868 Shepley was described as a township and chapelry in the parish of Kirkburton, upper division of Agbrigg Wapentake, West Riding County York. The village was also recorded as having 30 tailor's shops in a population of around 1,000. These would have sprung up as a result of the four mills around the village manufacturing fine woollen worsteds. The industrial development of the area continued into the late 19th and early 20th centuries, transforming the agricultural landscape into a more complex center of manufacturing. The textile industry, which had long been the economic backbone of Shepley, adapted to the new mechanized processes sweeping through British industry. The numerous small mills, initially geared towards the production of fine woollen worsteds, began to incorporate steam power and later, electrical power, allowing for larger output and greater specialization in fabric types. This economic shift necessitated changes in the local labor force, attracting workers from surrounding rural communities and other regions seeking employment in the burgeoning industrial sector. The infrastructure supporting this growth, including roads and canal access in earlier periods, became increasingly vital for transporting raw materials and finished goods. Later Victorian and Edwardian expansions saw the construction of more substantial housing to accommodate the growing population of mill workers and associated tradespeople. The local ecclesiastical structure, mentioned in the 1868 record, continued to serve the community, with the chapelry status reflecting the growing distinctiveness of the settlement within the broader parish structure. Local governance began to adapt to the needs of a more urbanized, industrially active community, moving beyond purely manorial administration to incorporate municipal functions as the village matured. The historical record thus shows a transition from a feudal, agricultural entity subject to manorial control to a more modern, industrially focused township integrated into the wider networks of Victorian and Edwardian commerce.

The film was also collected in a 10-disc box set titled "Marvel Cinematic Universe: Phase One – Avengers Assembled" which includes all of the Phase One films in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. It was released by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment on April 2, 2013. Universal released the film on Ultra HD Blu-ray on April 10, 2018. The Incredible Hulk began streaming on Disney+ in the United States on June 16, 2023, after the distribution rights to the film reverted to Marvel Studios and Disney from Universal. Reception Box office The Incredible Hulk earned $134.8 million in the United States and Canada, as well as $128.6 million from other territories, for a worldwide total of $263.4 million. The film, even though it barely passed its predecessor, and only equalled it if the smaller budget of the first film is taken into account, was still considered moderately successful. Entertainment analyst David Davis told The Hollywood Reporter, "The first Hulk had such high expectations after the NBCUniversal merger and was supposed to be critical-favorite Ang Lee's breakout commercial blockbuster. Then with the new Hulk film, Marvel was able to underplay the importance of the success after the great success of Iron Man this summer. So the new one overdelivered, relative to its underpromise." The Incredible Hulk earned $55.4 million in its opening weekend, becoming the top film at the box office. Behind Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer, it was the second-highest gross for a film released over the Father's Day weekend. This surpassed industry expectations of a $45 million opening, following the disappointing response to the 2003 film. Universal believed word of mouth would contribute to the film breaking even eventually. The Incredible Hulk also opened in 38 other countries, adding $31 million to the total opening. The film outgrossed the 2003 film in South Korea, while its openings in Mexico and Russia created records for Universal. The film grossed 24 million yuan (roughly $3.4 million) in its Chinese opening on August 26, outgrossing the previous film's overall gross of 10 million yuan. Critical response The review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reported an approval rating of , with an average score of , based on reviews. The critical response varied across different publications, with some reviewers praising the visual effects and the performance of Edward Norton, while others found the narrative underdeveloped or predictable. Some critics noted the film's adherence to the established MCU framework, viewing it as a necessary connective piece rather than a standalone cinematic achievement. Conversely, some praised its unique blend of superhero action with moments of genuine emotional weight regarding Bruce Banner's isolation. The film was generally seen as a functional entry into the burgeoning shared universe, providing adequate setup for future installments without achieving the cultural impact of its contemporaries. Awards consideration was minimal, as the film did not receive nominations at major industry ceremonies. Its placement within the overarching Marvel narrative allowed it to be viewed less as a singular artistic endeavor and more as a building block in a larger cinematic tapestry. This approach meant that while it was commercially viable, it did not attract the same level of critical fervor as films with more ambitious standalone narratives. The continued success of the MCU in the subsequent years would ultimately redefine how these mid-tier entries were perceived by audiences and critics alike.

In 1953, Parsons asked Pitts to join him in England to work on the projected book: Theories of Society. co-authored by T. Shils, Kaspar Naegele and Jesse R. The book was published in 1961 and became a standard text for Sociology students. Pitts received his Ph.D. in 1958 and began his teaching career in Detroit, Michigan, at Wayne State University, as assistant professor, then as associate professor. In 1964, he left for Oakland University, in Rochester Michigan, where he taught from 1964 to 1986, as full professor and chairman. He taught at the Harvard Summer School in 1971 and 1975. He was twice a Fulbright Fellow. During a long stay in Paris (1966–1968) he was a lecturer at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes (Paris-Sorbonne). While living in Paris he participated in Television broadcasts and wrote newspapers articles. He wrote a book on the 1968 May events in France, but decided against publishing it. A perfectionist, he put aside many works that did not satisfy him. Politically, while Pitts had held left wing views in his youth, he shifted to more conservative opinions. Almost all of his friends and colleagues were liberal intellectuals and solid Democrats (Democratic Party (United States)), but Pitts was never reticent to debate issues, often appearing on talk shows and as a columnist for various publications. The Tocqueville Review Pitts founded The Tocqueville Review/La Revue Tocqueville in 1978 and was its editor until 1991. The Review is a French-American bilingual journal devoted to the comparative study of social change in the spirit of Alexis de Tocqueville's pioneer investigations. Pitts recruited many of his colleagues to author essays on current affairs, history, and political philosophy. In 2003, at the memorial event in Charlottesville, Professor Ted Caplow, first president and founder of the Tocqueville Society, defined the review as:"...a proud monument and one that will long honor him." Caplow also said: "...its intellectual standards are exceptionally high and it continues to attract contributions, both in English and French, from major scholars and public figures on both sides of the Atlantic." Pitts was a member of the Tocqueville Jury which awarded the Prix Alexis de Tocqueville to international scholars. His engagement with Tocqueville suggested a deep commitment to the enduring questions of democracy, civic life, and societal evolution in modern contexts. The journal served as a platform for rigorous intellectual exchange, bridging American and French sociological and political thought. Throughout his later career, Pitts continued to engage with themes of social stratification, institutional stability, and the nature of political participation, often drawing upon classical sociological theory to analyze contemporary phenomena. His scholarly output, though selective, demonstrated a consistent preoccupation with how social structures mediate individual agency. He maintained a vibrant intellectual presence within academic circles, frequently participating in symposia and advising younger scholars on research methodologies and theoretical grounding. The transition in his political leanings did not equate to a withdrawal from public discourse; rather, it informed a more nuanced and critical engagement with the prevailing political narratives of the time. His contributions to the Tocqueville Review often exhibited this measured, dialectical approach, presenting complex arguments without succumbing to simplistic ideological pronouncements. The journal’s success reflected Pitts’s ability to attract contributors whose work was sophisticated, multifaceted, and deeply researched. His involvement in the Tocqueville Society underscored his dedication not merely to abstract theory, but to fostering a community of scholars dedicated to the practical and philosophical study of democratic societies. Later years saw him continue to mentor doctoral candidates, instilling in them the importance of methodological rigor alongside broad theoretical comprehension. His legacy is thus multifaceted, encompassing his foundational work in the sociology of theory, his editorial stewardship of a significant international intellectual journal, and his lifelong dedication to probing the mechanisms of modern civic life.

Proposed pathophysiological mechanisms include seizure-induced cardiac and respiratory arrests. Among epileptics, SUDEP occurs in about 1 in 1,000 adults and 1 in 4,500 children annually. Rates of death as a result of prolonged seizures (status epilepticus) are not classified as SUDEP. Categories The overarching term SUDEP can be subdivided into four different categories: Definite, Probably, Possible, and Unlikely. Definite SUDEP: a non-traumatic and non-drowning death in an individual with epilepsy, without a cause of death after postmortem examination. Definite SUDEP Plus: includes the presence of a concomitant condition other than epilepsy, where death may be due to the combined effects of both epilepsy and the other condition. Probably SUDEP: all the same criteria for Definite SUDEP are met, but no postmortem examination is performed. Possible SUDEP: insufficient information is available regarding the death, with no postmortem examination. Unlikely SUDEP: an alternate cause of death has been determined, ruling out the possibility of SUDEP being the cause. Risk factors Consistent risk factors include: Severity of seizures, increased refractoriness of epilepsy and presence of generalized tonic–clonic seizures: the most consistent risk factor is an increased frequency of tonic–clonic seizures. Lack of therapeutic levels of anti-epileptic drugs, non-adherence to treatment regimens and frequent changes in regimens are risk factors for sudden death. Young age and early age of seizures onset Male sex Being asleep during a seizure is likely to favour SUDEP occurrence. Genetic mutations have been identified that increase a person's risk for SUDEP (some are discussed below), but ultimately their genetic risk is determined by the function of multiple genes that is not yet well understood. Overlap is seen between these ion channel genes and the different sudden death disorders, including SUDEP, SIDS, sudden unexpected death (SUD), and sudden unexplained death in childhood (SUDC). Many of the genes are involved in long QT syndrome. Mutations in the KCNQ1 gene that codes for the voltage-gated potassium channel KV7.1 have been implicated in cardiac arrhythmias, such as long QT syndrome 1 (LQT1), and epilepsy. Mutations in potassium channel gene KCNH2 have been identified with LQT2. Mutations in sodium channel gene SCN5A have been identified with LQT3. Mutations in potassium channel gene KCNJ2 have been identified with LQT7. Mutations in calcium channel gene CACNA1C have been identified with LQT8. The investigation into these genetic predispositions continues to reveal complex interactions between neuronal excitability and cardiac electrophysiology. Certain genetic variations can compromise the stability of the cellular membrane, leading to abnormal firing patterns in both brain cells and heart muscle cells. The precise mechanisms linking these ion channel dysfunctions to the terminal events of SUDEP remain an area of intensive biomedical research. Understanding how impaired potassium, sodium, or calcium channel function contributes to the cascade leading to cardiac or respiratory failure is paramount for developing targeted preventative strategies. While statistical associations are strong, establishing a direct, causal pathway between a specific mutation and the development of SUDEP in an individual remains a significant clinical challenge. Further longitudinal studies incorporating advanced neuroimaging and continuous cardiac monitoring in high-risk populations are essential to refine risk stratification tools. Current research efforts are also exploring the role of autonomic nervous system dysregulation in the context of epilepsy, positing that altered control over heart rate and respiration during or immediately following a seizure event may be a critical intermediary step toward SUDEP. Interventions aiming to stabilize autonomic function alongside seizure control are therefore emerging as promising therapeutic avenues. For instance, medications that modulate vagal tone or those designed to stabilize cardiac pacemaker activity are being evaluated in epilepsy patients, particularly those with a history of recurrent, prolonged seizures. The distinction between SUDEP and death resulting from other seizure complications, such as severe cerebral injury or metabolic derangement, requires meticulous clinical documentation, which is often lacking in postmortem reports. Epidemiological data continues to guide public health initiatives, emphasizing the necessity of rigorous epilepsy management protocols, adherence to prescribed pharmacotherapy, and prompt recognition of seizure exacerbations to mitigate the risk of sudden, unexplained mortality.

Other serious side effects may include fungal infections, anaphylaxis, and muscle weakness. It is unclear if use during pregnancy is safe for the baby. Polymyxin B works by breaking down the cytoplasmic membrane which generally results in bacterial cell death. Polymyxin B was approved for medical use in the United States in 1964. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is available as a generic medication. In Europe it is only approved to be applied to the skin as of 2015. It is derived from the bacterium Paenibacillus polymyxa (formerly known as Bacillus polymyxa). Medical uses Spectrum of susceptibility Polymyxin B has been used to treat urinary tract infections and meningitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae, respectively. The following represents MIC susceptibility data for a few medically significant microorganisms. Haemophilus influenzae: ≥0.8 μg/mL Pseudomonas aeruginosa: 0.25–1 μg/mL Endotoxin adsorption An effective use of polymyxin B is found in patients with refractory septic shock, that is, without positive outcome to the administration of standard treatments (increase in volemia and other antibiotics). The obstacle of the toxicity of polymyxin B is bypassed by extracorporeal circulation with perfusion of venous blood through a cartridge on whose fibers polymyxin B is covalently fixed; in this way the antibiotic exerts its bactericidal function but is not released into the blood since it remains fully attached to the fiber. Through this perfusion the cartridge retains the endotoxin, recognized as the trigger of septic shock. The treatment of the cartridge to polymyxin B (Toraymyxin, medical device designed and produced by the Japanese Toray), takes place in two sessions of two hours each, carried out at a distance of 24 hours. Mechanism of action Alters bacterial outer membrane permeability by binding to a negatively charged site in the lipopolysaccharide layer, which has an electrostatic attraction for the positively charged amino groups in the cyclic peptide portion (this site normally is a binding site for calcium and magnesium counter ions); the result is a destabilized outer membrane Fatty acid portion dissolves in hydrophobic region of cytoplasmic membrane and disrupts membrane integrity Leakage of cellular molecules, inhibition of cellular respiration Binds and inactivates endotoxin Relative absence of selective toxicity: nonspecific for cell membranes of any type, highly toxic. Its broad action against various cell membranes underscores its lack of specificity, a characteristic that contributes significantly to its observed toxicity in mammalian systems. Clinical applications are therefore carefully managed, often requiring stringent monitoring of patient vital signs and renal function. Alternative antimicrobial agents are frequently sought when polymyxin B is contraindicated or when the risk-benefit profile is deemed unfavorable. Research continues into novel delivery systems and modified derivatives of polymyxin B to mitigate systemic side effects while preserving antimicrobial efficacy. The structural integrity of the bacterial cell wall is a common target for antibiotics, yet polymyxin B represents a unique approach by targeting the outer membrane structure of Gram-negative bacteria. The disruption of this outer membrane allows subsequent damage to the inner cytoplasmic membrane, leading to cellular collapse and death. This pathway differs from antibiotics that interfere with peptidoglycan synthesis, such as penicillin derivatives. The ability of polymyxin B to bind to and sequester endotoxin is another critical function, providing a benefit beyond direct bacterial killing, particularly in severe inflammatory states like septic shock. This endotoxin sequestration prevents the uncontrolled release of lipopolysaccharide into the bloodstream, which is a major driver of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome associated with Gram-negative infections. The commercial availability and regional approval status of the drug vary significantly between different healthcare jurisdictions, impacting global access to this established therapeutic agent.

During the German-Soviet War he was responsible for putting the economy on a war footing. In 1942, he was co-opted onto the State Defense Committee, and was again chairman of Gosplan, 1942-49. On 20 August 1945, after the Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, he was appointed to the Special Committee on the use of Atomic Energy, which was responsible for developing a Soviet atomic bomb. Post World War II After the war, Voznesensky resumed his position as a Deputy Chairman of the Council of Ministers. In March 1946, he presented the first post-war Five Year Plan. In October 1946, in an incident that later formed part of Nikita Khrushchev's seminal Secret Speech to the 20th party congress, Voznesensky was co-opted onto the 'Politburo Commission for Foreign Affairs' whose remit was being expanded to include 'internal construction and domestic policy' The implication is that Stalin created this committee as a way of excluding certain members of the Politburo from the decision making process, including his eventual successor, Georgy Malenkov, who was temporarily out of favour. From February 28, 1947 to March 7, 1949 Voznesensky was a full member of the Politburo of the All-Union Communist Party. In December 1947, he published his major work, The Wartime Economy of the USSR during the Great Patriotic War, which won him a Stalin Prize, and 200,000 ruble prize. In it, he forecast that as a result of the absorbing of Eastern Europe into the Soviet sphere of influence "the general crisis of capitalism has become more acute", that the high level of productivity achieved in the USA during the war would be followed by "a new devastating economic crisis and chronic unemployment" and that "having waxed fat on the people's blood during the Second World War, monopoly capitalism of the USA stands now at the head the anti-democratic camp ... and has become the instigator of imperialist expansion everywhere." The book was a refutation of the views of the Hungarian economist, Eugen Varga, who forecast a softening of some of the harsher features of capitalism, and argued that the East European countries occupied by the Red Army did not amount to a huge loss to world capitalism. His analysis of international economic trends reflected the prevailing Soviet ideological stance against Western capitalist systems. Voznesensky's economic theories were deeply embedded within the framework of Marxist-Leninist doctrine, emphasizing the inherent contradictions and ultimate collapse of market economies. His pronouncements served not only as academic contributions but also as instruments of state policy, reinforcing the narrative of the inevitable triumph of socialist planning over capitalist volatility. During the late 1940s, his influence grew within the planning apparatus, providing the intellectual justification for the centralized command economy being implemented across the Soviet Union. This system relied on Gosplan to dictate production quotas, resource allocation, and investment priorities, a structure that Voznesensky helped to refine and solidify in the immediate post-war environment. Despite his high standing within the Party and the state apparatus, Voznesensky's career trajectory exhibited the inherent volatility of high-level Soviet bureaucracy, where political favor often superseded technical competence. His subsequent political positioning became increasingly complex as Stalin's grip on absolute power began to loosen following his death in 1953. The shift in leadership brought about a period of internal reorganization within the Party and government, affecting the roles and perceived importance of numerous technocrats like Voznesensky. His later activities involved advisory roles related to industrial modernization and the execution of Five Year Plan directives, though his central planning authority was never fully reinstated to its pre-war stature. He remained a figure of considerable, if sometimes behind-the-scenes, influence in Soviet economic discourse until the later years of the Khrushchev and Brezhnev eras.

His bride was the legendary beauty Gayatri Devi of Cooch Behar, the daughter of Maharaja Jitendra Narayan of Cooch Behar and Maharani Indira Devi, princess of Baroda. She stands out among the Maharanis of Jaipur for having become a public figure and a celebrity of sorts, initially for being a fashion-conscious beauty and later for becoming a politician and parliamentarian. Devi survived him by thirty-nine years, dying in 2009. Children Man Singh was the father of four sons and a daughter, borne to him by his three wives. They were: By his first wife, Maharani Marudhar Kunwar, one son and one daughter Prem Kumari (1929–1970). In 1948, she was given in marriage to the Maharawal of Baria. Bhawani Singh (1931–2011), succeeded to his father's title in 1970. In 1967, he married Padmini Devi, daughter of the Raja of Sirmur, and had one daughter; Diya Kumari (b. 1970). She has three children, including one son who was adopted by Bhawani Singh and declared his successor, namely: Padmanabh Singh (b. 1998). Born a commoner, he was declared royal and adopted by his maternal grandfather in 2002. By his second wife, Maharani Kishore Kunwar, two sons Jai Singh (b. 1933). he was given the title of Raja of Jhalai and the estate of Jhalai in appanage by his father. In 1983, he married Vidya Devi, daughter of the Raja of Jubbal, and has one son. Ajay Singh Prithviraj (1935–2020); received the title Raja of Bhagwatgarth. In 1961, he married Devika Devi, a princess of Tripura and a niece (sister's daughter) of his step-mother Gayatri Devi. They had been living separately from each other by the time she died in 2009, a few months before her aunt. Gayatri Devi tended to support her step-son and deprecate her niece in the matter of their marital differences, and Prithviraj Singh remained close to his step-mother all his life. The Jaipur royal family, like many princely states in India, experienced a gradual transition from absolute monarchies to constitutional roles following the integration of princely states into the Indian Union in the mid-twentieth century. This shift significantly altered the traditional functions and public visibility of the ruling families. The administrative and political roles previously held by the Maharajas were either absorbed by state governments or transformed into advisory capacities within the federal structure. Members of the royal houses often navigated this complex sociopolitical landscape, maintaining a public presence while adapting to modern governance. The continuation of their influence, even in diminished forms, often relied upon their historical legacy, land holdings, and social networks. Succession within these families was traditionally governed by complex rules of primogeniture, although the integration process sometimes necessitated adjustments or interpretations of these ancient customs. The personal lives of these prominent figures frequently intersected with public interest due to their lineage and former stature. The relationships described, such as the evolving dynamics between Gayatri Devi and her extended family members, illustrate the intricate personal currents that ran alongside the grand institutional changes affecting the royal houses. The continuation of the royal presence in contemporary India is thus a blend of inherited tradition and modern societal expectations.

During the Sevier orogeny mountain-building event about 115 and 55 million years ago, what is known as the Cordilleran foreland thrust-and-fold event occurred along the east side of the Rocky Mountains in northwest Montana. The thrust-and-fold belt does not extend all the way south through Montana. Instead, it cuts west above Three Forks continues south—crossing the Snake River Plain and skirting the west side of the Colorado Plateau before cutting west again to enter California. Although most of this mountain-building has since been obliterated by additional orogeny and volcanic activity, most of it still exists in northwestern Montana. The Rocky Mountain Front in this area represents some of the highest changes of elevation within a short distance anywhere in North America. Much of this part of the front, including the Lewis Range and Livingston Range, has suffered heavy glaciation.
