The range of programming reflects an organizational commitment to holistic community development, extending beyond mere entertainment to encompass cultural education and social commentary. The inclusion of both Irish and English language programming in Draíocht reflects an awareness of the linguistic landscape of Northern Ireland and its importance in promoting inclusive participation. Féile an Phobail's efforts to present a broad spectrum of artistic expression—from traditional music to contemporary stand-up comedy—aim to appeal to the widest possible segment of the populace. The hosting of internationally acclaimed musicians alongside local talent underscores a desire to place regional culture within a broader global context. Furthermore, the invitation of prominent journalists and political figures to participate in panel discussions transforms the festival grounds into a space for public intellectual engagement. This blending of high culture, community celebration, and political discourse characterizes the unique cultural footprint of these initiatives in the region. The ongoing operation of these varied projects demonstrates a sustained investment in social cohesion through the medium of the arts.

In her family, the young princess was nicknamed "Mariechen" (a possible homage to her parents' German heritage) or "Itty" (derived from little). Everyone who knew Maria described her as a beautiful and precocious young child, as she was said to look at maps and identify different countries for fun at the age of only two and a half. It is said that sometime before she died, Princess Maria told her mother that she would someday like to be able to ride a star. Maria had no prospect of inheriting her father's throne; the 1866 Constitution limited succession to males. Death On , the Princess became ill with scarlet fever. An epidemic had been ravaging the capital at the time. She was immediately transported to the Peleș Castle. Despite being treated with much care by a doctor named Theodori and many others, the young princess died on and was buried at the monastery of Cotroceni. At Elisabeth's request, Maria's tombstone read the Bible verse, : The funeral service took place at the Cotroceni Church within the grounds of the Cotroceni Royal Palace. The coffin was covered with white satin, criss-crossed with silver lace ornaments and was as large as one for an adult, because the infant princess' body was enclosed in several decreasing size caskets placed one inside another. After the religious service in the Romanian Orthodox rite, the cortege walked through the palace gardens to the burial place next to the palace church. Those gardens were the favorite playing grounds for the young princess, where only half a dozen days previously she had played with her nurse. Legacy Maria's parents were devastated by her death. On 5 May that year, Carol wrote to his father Karl Anton, Prince of Hohenzollern, that he and Elisabeth intended to move to the Cotroceni Palace, in order to be closer to the resting place of their infant daughter: In another letter to Lascăr Catargiu, he wrote: Maria's death worsened the relationship between Carol and Elisabeth, and they did not have any further children. In 1875, Karl Storck created a bust of the sleeping princess which was erected by her tomb. This bust inspired Elisabeth to write many emotional poems. When Queen Elisabeth died in 1916, according to her wishes, her daughter's remains were exhumed and the casket placed on her coffin for the public procession. Mother and daughter were then buried together in the same tomb at the Cathedral of Curtea de Argeș. At the Elisabeta Palace, one can still see an 1880s style piece of furniture that contains a plaster-mold of the infant princess. This small artifact serves as a poignant memento of the young royal figure. The preservation of such personal items underscores the enduring impact of Maria on the lives of her parents, particularly Elisabeth. Her early life, characterized by precociousness and a childlike wonder evident in her stated desire to ride a star, contrasts sharply with the sudden fragility of her health. The scarlet fever outbreak represented a significant public health crisis within the capital at the time, lending a tragic backdrop to her final days. Her interment at Cotroceni was a private, deeply felt ceremony, marked by elaborate honors befitting a member of royalty, even one so young. The subsequent decision by Carol and Elisabeth to relocate to the Cotroceni Palace further illustrates the profound grief and desire for proximity to their lost child. The creation of the sculpted likeness by Karl Storck was not merely a memorial but a catalyst for Elisabeth's artistic expression, channeling her sorrow into poetry. The eventual reburial alongside her mother in the venerable Cathedral of Curtea de Argeș represents the culmination of their desire to unite their loved ones in a place of significant national and religious importance. The furniture piece remaining at the Elisabeta Palace continues to offer a tangible link to this tender, yet tragically brief, chapter of Romanian royal history.

As such, the name N. eymae holds nomenclatural priority and N. infundibuliformis is considered a heterotypic synonym. A similar situation involved the descriptions of N. glabrata and N. hamata by the same authors. Turnbull and Middleton's description is based on the specimen J.R.Turnbull & A.T.Middleton 83148a, which was collected by the authors on September 20, 1983, from Mount Lumut Kecil in Sulawesi at the coordinates , at an altitude of 1500 m. In their description of the species, Turnbull and Middleton stated that the type material was deposited at Herbarium Bogoriense (BO), the herbarium of the Bogor Botanical Gardens, but Matthew Jebb and Martin Cheek were unable to locate it and wrote that it "appear not to have been deposited at Bogor as stated". In addition to the herbarium specimens of N. eymae mentioned here, a number of others have appeared in the literature. Most authors regard N. eymae as a distinct species and it has been treated as such in all major monographs on the genus, including Matthew Jebb and Martin Cheek's "A skeletal revision of Nepenthes (Nepenthaceae)" (1997) and "Nepenthaceae" (2001), as well as Stewart McPherson's Pitcher Plants of the Old World (2009). Nonetheless, some authors have expressed doubt that it merits distinction from N. maxima at the species level. In Pitcher Plants of the Old World, McPherson wrote that "the specific status of N. eymae seems warranted since the two taxa appear to occur both together and in isolated, self-sustaining communities". Whatever the status of this taxon, the vast majority of plants cultivated under the name N. eymae do not exhibit the abruptly contracted upper pitchers commonly associated with it. Description Nepenthes eymae is a climbing plant growing to a height of up to 8 m. The stem, which may be branched, is two-ridged and up to 8 mm in diameter. Internodes are up to 6 cm long. Axillary buds, which are found 3–10 mm above the leaf axils in climbing stems, are spike-like and measure up to 10 mm (rarely 20 mm) in length by 1.5 mm in width. Leaves are coriaceous and petiolate. The lamina (leaf blade) is oblong or oblong-elliptic and reaches up to 35 cm in length by 12 cm in width. The laminar apex is rounded or acute to obtuse and is not peltate. The base is obtuse and attenuate, narrowing to form a petiole. The petiole is canaliculate and occasionally winged, the wings being around 4 mm wide. The pitchers are typically urn-shaped or cylindrical, generally ranging from 6 to 15 cm in height. They possess a distinct peristome that is often flared and crenulate. The color of the pitchers can vary significantly depending on the growing conditions and age of the plant, ranging from green to reddish-brown. The peristome exhibits variations in ribbing and coloration across different populations. The lid, or operculum, is generally ovate to oblong, sometimes slightly reflexed at the margins, and is characterized by prominent nectar glands. These glands are usually arranged in a pattern across the underside of the lid. Reproduction in Nepenthes species occurs through sexual means, involving pollination followed by seed set, although vegetative propagation through stem cuttings is also common in cultivation. The ecological preferences of N. eymae are associated with montane habitats, typically found in mossy, well-drained forest understories. Its distribution is currently known from limited areas within Sulawesi, although further fieldwork is required to fully map its range. Conservation status assessments are ongoing, given the relatively limited data available regarding its wild populations and habitat specificity. The collection and study of this species contribute to the understanding of pitcher plant diversity in Southeast Asia.

Notes Per country The yellow jersey has been awarded to 25 countries since 1903. In the table below, "Jerseys" indicates the number of yellow jerseys that were given to cyclists of each country. "Tour wins" stands for the number of tour wins by cyclists of that country, "Points" for the number of times the points classification was won by cyclist of that country, "Mountains" for the number of times the mountains classification in the Tour de France was won by a cyclist of that country, and "Young rider" for the number of times the young rider classification was won by a cyclist of that country. The "Most recent holder" column shows the cyclist of the country that wore the yellow jersey most recently. The "Different holders" column gives the number of cyclists of the country that wore the yellow jersey. Yellow jersey retirees There have been sixteen instances where a rider quit the Tour for any reason while wearing the yellow jersey. Yellow jersey winners with no stage wins Usually the winner of the Tour de France also wins at least one stage, but that is not necessary. It is possible to win the Tour de France without winning a single stage, because the overall winner of the Tour de France is decided solely by the total race time. This has happened eight times so far: 1922 1956 1960 1966 1990 2006 2017 2019 Of these eight cyclists, Walkowiak and Bernal are the only ones never to win a Tour stage at all, although Bernal is still active as of 2022, and was leading solo in the final stages of a stage abandoned due to a landslide on the final kilometres of the course in 2019, the year he won the Tour. Firmin Lambot won stages in the 1913, 1914, 1919, 1920 and 1921 Tours, Gastone Nencini won stages in the 1956, 1957 and 1958 Tours, Aimar won a stage in the 1967 Tour, LeMond won stages in the 1985, 1986 and 1989 Tours, Pereiro won a stage in the 2005 Tour, and Froome won stages in the 2012, 2013, 2015 and 2016 Tours. Alberto Contador initially also belonged to this group, when he won the 2010 Tour de France; however, he was later stripped of this title. Number of Tour winners in a single race Every Tour de France only has one winner. But a cyclist that has won the Tour de France previously can enter the race again, and a cyclist not winning the race can win the race in a later year. Records for multiple Tour victories are tracked separately from the individual achievements listed above. Several riders have accumulated multiple victories throughout their careers, demonstrating sustained excellence over many years of competitive racing. The record for the most Tour de France victories held by a single rider is currently shared by a few athletes. These riders have showcased exceptional endurance and tactical acumen across various editions of the race. The accumulation of these titles often reflects not only physical prowess but also the ability to adapt to changing course conditions and competitive landscapes over decades. Moreover, some riders managed to secure their victories in vastly different eras of cycling, encountering varying technological advancements in equipment and evolving sporting methodologies. The consistency required to maintain a high level of performance over such an extended period is considered one of the greatest feats in professional cycling. This longevity allows for a broader comparative analysis of how the sport has developed from its early iterations to its modern, highly professionalized form. The sustained dominance of certain figures provides benchmarks against which subsequent generations of competitors are measured.

Dornach is also a quarter of the French city of Mulhouse and the Scots name for Dornoch in the Scottish Highlands, and Dòrnach is the Gaelic name for Dornoch in the Scottish Highlands. Dornach (Swiss German: Dornech) is a municipality in the district of Dorneck in the canton of Solothurn in Switzerland. History Dornach is first mentioned in 1223 as de Tornacho. In 1307 it was mentioned as zu Dornach. It has been settled since at least 1223 when a local lay priest was known as Johannes de Tornacho (thought to mean "from the estate of Turnus"). The site was the location of the decisive 1499 Battle of Dornach, which ended the Swabian War and effectively ensured the independence of the Old Swiss Confederacy from the Holy Roman Empire. The battle is memorialized in a 1949 relief wall. Today Dornach is famous for the Goetheanum and is home to the international headquarters of the Anthroposophical movement founded by Rudolf Steiner. Geography Dornach has an area, , of . Of this area, or 17.3% is used for agricultural purposes, while or 46.3% is forested. Of the rest of the land, or 35.5% is settled (buildings or roads), or 0.3% is either rivers or lakes and or 0.2% is unproductive land. Of the built-up area, industrial buildings made up 3.6% of the total area while housing and buildings made up 22.4% and transportation infrastructure made up 6.8%. while parks, green belts and sports fields made up 2.3%. Out of the forested land, 44.2% of the total land area is heavily forested and 2.1% is covered with orchards or small clusters of trees. Of the agricultural land, 6.1% is used for growing crops and 8.0% is pastures, while 3.3% is used for orchards or vine crops. All the water in the municipality is flowing water. The municipality is in the Dorneck district. It consists of the village of Dornach which is made up of two villages, Dornachdorf (also known as Oberdornach) and Dornachbrugg. Until the last quarter of the 19th century the two villages were completely separate. Coat of arms The blazon of the municipal coat of arms is Argent two Fish-hooks inverted and addorsed Sable. Demographics Dornach has a population () of . , 23.8% of the population are resident foreign nationals. Over the last 10 years (1999–2009 ) the population has changed at a rate of 4.2%. Most of the population () speaks German (5,212 or 88.5%), with Italian being second most common (137 or 2.3%) and French being third (91 or 1.5%). The local economy of Dornach has traditionally been rooted in agriculture and small-scale industry, though the presence of the Goetheanum has introduced a significant element of cultural tourism. The infrastructure supports a moderate level of commercial activity catering both to local residents and international visitors drawn to the Anthroposophical center. Residential areas are interspersed with open green spaces, reflecting the municipality's integration of natural landscapes within its settled zones. The local administrative structure operates within the framework of the Canton of Solothurn, adhering to cantonal regulations regarding planning and environmental management. The railway connection provides Dornach with essential links to larger Swiss urban centers, facilitating both commuting and the transportation of goods related to its diverse economic base. The geological substrate of the region is characterized by glacial deposits, which influence the soil composition and suitability for different types of cultivation noted in the land use statistics. Conservation efforts are continually managed to preserve the heavily forested areas, which serve ecological functions within the municipality. Furthermore, the historical significance attached to the 1499 battle contributes to the local identity and attracts historical interest, complementing the modern cultural draw of the Goetheanum.

On the upper first molar, one accessory ridge, the anteroloph, is lacking, but another, the mesoloph, is present. Unlike in most other oryzomyines, however, which have mesolophs reaching the labial margin of the molar, the mesolophs of Pseudoryzomys are short and protrude only slightly from the middle of the molar. The corresponding structure in the lower molars, the mesolophid, is completely absent. The hindmost valley between cusps on the lower first molar, the posteroflexid, is severely reduced, foreshadowing its loss in Lundomys and Holochilus. A number of molar traits support Pseudoryzomyss relationship with Holochilus and Lundomys, forming steps in the transition from the complex, low-crowned generalized oryzomyine molar pattern to the simpler, high-crowned pattern of Holochilus. As in all oryzomyines, the upper molars all have one root on the inner (lingual) side and two on the outer (labial) side; in addition, the first upper molar in Pseudoryzomys and some other species has another labial root. The first lower molar has large roots at the front and back of the tooth and two smaller ones in between, at the labial and lingual side. The second and third lowers molars have two roots at the front, one labial and one lingual, and another at the back. Postcranial skeleton Pseudoryzomys has 19 or 20 thoracic (chest) and lumbar vertebrae, 13 of which bear ribs, as is characteristic of oryzomyines. The first ribs contact both the seventh cervical (neck) vertebra and the first thoracic vertebra, an important character of the Sigmodontinae. Unlike in most sigmodontines, including Holochilus and Lundomys, the fourth lumbar vertebra lacks the processes known as anapophyses. There are three or four sacral and about 29 caudal (tail) vertebrae. Between the second and third caudal vertebrae, separate bones called hemal arches are present. These display a spinous process at the back, as in both Holochilus and Lundomys. On the humerus, the upper arm bone, the entepicondylar foramen is absent, as in all members of the Sigmodontinae; in some other cricetids, it perforates the far (distal) end of the humerus. Karyotype The karyotype generally includes 56 chromosomes with a total of 54 major arms (2n = 56, FN = 54) in specimens from both Bolivia and Brazil; a poorly prepared Paraguayan specimen seems to have a similar karyotype. In this karyotype, all autosomes (non-sex chromosomes) are acrocentric (with one arm so short as to be almost invisible). However, in two specimens from the Brazilian states of Tocantins and São Paulo, one pair of autosomes contains both an acrocentric and a metacentric chromosome (with two equally long arms), yielding an FN of 55. This variation in karyotype suggests possible intraspecific or population-level variation within the genus. The acrocentric nature of the autosomes is a common feature among many rodent groups, indicating a general evolutionary trend within the family Cricetidae, though the specific arrangement is taxonomically relevant for differentiating genera. Further cytogenetic analysis, including detailed examination of chromosome morphology and banding patterns, is necessary to definitively resolve the placement of Pseudoryzomys relative to its proposed allies, Holochilus and Lundomys. The combination of dental features, particularly the incomplete mesoloph structure, and the vertebral characteristics, such as the absence of anapophyses on the fourth lumbar vertebra, provides a mosaic of traits linking it to lineages undergoing evolutionary simplification in molar morphology. The transition from the complex cuspidate pattern seen in ancestral oryzomyines towards the simpler, high-crowned morphology observed in derived forms like Holochilus reflects a significant adaptive shift, potentially related to dietary changes or habitat specialization. The presence of hemal arches between the caudal vertebrae is a shared, derived trait within this clade, reinforcing its close relationship to other members of the Sigmodontinae subfamily. Comparative study of skull metrics, such as the zygomatic breadth and rostrum length, offers additional osteological data points for robust phylogenetic reconstruction beyond the scope of dental and skeletal counts alone.

Animation and its various subgenres encompass a broad spectrum of visual storytelling, ranging from traditional hand-drawn cel animation to sophisticated computer-generated imagery. The evolution of animation technology has profoundly influenced its aesthetic possibilities and narrative complexity. Early forms of animation, such as those produced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, were often simple, focusing on basic motion and novelty. The development of synchronized sound in the mid-20th century marked a significant turning point, allowing animated characters to engage in dialogue and complex musical numbers, thereby elevating the medium's potential for dramatic and comedic effect. Post-war animation saw the rise of various national styles, with Japanese animation, or anime, developing a distinct visual language characterized by detailed character design, dynamic action sequences, and deep thematic explorations. Simultaneously, Western animation continued to diversify, moving beyond purely comedic shorts into feature-length narratives addressing mature subjects. The transition to digital production in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries revolutionized the industry, offering unprecedented control over color, texture, and movement. This technological shift has facilitated the creation of highly detailed and complex animated worlds, impacting everything from mainstream family fare to critically acclaimed independent works. Modern animation serves as a versatile medium capable of engaging audiences across all demographics while pushing the boundaries of visual artistry and narrative sophistication.

Production Ryan was shot entirely on film and in colour with an eye to potential international sales. An initial sale of 39 episodes to the Seven Network recouped only 55% of the series' relatively high production costs. An international sale was therefore crucial to the show's continued feasibility. Australian television was still in the process of transitioning to colour broadcasting in 1973, while key international markets were already in colour and would more readily purchase a colour series. Though many Australian series shot their interior scenes on videotape in the studio using a multiple-camera setup with only outdoor scenes shot on film, many television studios were not yet equipped with colour equipment. This meant Ryan had to be shot entirely on film. In another concession to international marketability Mullinar was instructed to play the role using a Mid-Atlantic American accent. The series premiered in May 1973, rating well in Brisbane and Adelaide, but failing in the crucial Melbourne and Sydney markets. A key reason for low ratings was the fact that the Nine Network had moved the highly popular police drama Division 4 to a new night to compete with the much-hyped new series. Ryan was moved around the schedules in order to find an audience, but ratings remained mediocre. After the initial 39 episodes were in the can the Ryan crew were, in expectation of a second series, retained by Crawfords and put to work on Homicide - whose output was increased to two episodes a week - on that show's second weekly episode. This resulted in one cross-over episode, with the Ryan regular characters appearing in an episode of Homicide. One regular cast member, Pamela Stephenson, did not appear, having opted to leave the series during the recess. Ultimately Ryan was not renewed by the Seven Network due to insufficient ratings. The Homicide production reverted to one episode a week. While some of the Ryan crew were rolled into new Crawfords serial The Box, that show featured little outdoors filming so inevitably some of the Ryan crew were retrenched - the first time Crawfords had ever retrenched staff. Cast Main Rod Mullinar as Michael Ryan Pamela Stephenson as Julie King Luigi Villani as Tony Angelini Colin McEwan as Detective Cullen Guests Peter Gwynne as Raymond Fitch Kevin Miles as John Hiller Terry McDermott Penne Hackforth-Jones as Jana / Helen (2 episodes) Diane Craig as Lacey Glen (1 episode) Anthony Hawkins Episodes DVD release The complete series was released on DVD in June 2018. The series' format presented a unique challenge for the production team, balancing the desire for a polished, international aesthetic with the practical limitations of the domestic broadcast environment. The reliance on full-length film stock, while costly, guaranteed the highest visual quality achievable at the time, a necessary prerequisite for securing lucrative overseas distribution deals. The mid-Atlantic accent requirement placed considerable demands on the actors, necessitating rigorous coaching to achieve a convincing transatlantic cadence without sounding overly artificial for the Australian viewing public. Despite the meticulous efforts to optimize the show for various markets, the entrenched viewing habits and competitive scheduling within the dominant metropolitan areas proved insurmountable obstacles. The financial investment, coupled with the fluctuating audience reception, led the network to a strategic decision against further commitment to the property. The transition of personnel to other productions like Homicide demonstrated the industry's tendency to redeploy experienced crews rather than entirely disbanding them following the cancellation of a single series. The Box, while offering employment, represented a departure from the genre and visual style that had defined Ryan, further illustrating the creative fragmentation that often occurs within a production house during periods of uncertain investment. The retrospective DVD release decades later provided a means for modern audiences to examine the series' distinctive production values and casting choices outside the context of its original broadcast struggles.

The selection demonstrates a broad geographical and stylistic reach, encompassing major figures from the Anglo-American literary tradition alongside significant contributors from continental Europe. The inclusion of both established masters and more contemporary voices reflects an attempt to capture the breadth of modern poetic expression. The American poets listed, such as Gwendolyn Brooks and Randall Jarrell, represent varying regional and thematic concerns within the United States. The French poets presented showcase diverse movements, from the surrealist tendencies of some to the more classically structured verse of others. The anthology's scope suggests an interest not merely in linguistic proficiency but in the cultural dialogues occurring across diverse literary landscapes during the mid-twentieth century. Further examination of the collected works would likely reveal thematic threads concerning modern alienation, political upheaval, and the evolving relationship between the individual and the industrial or natural world. The organizational structure, moving from prominent English-language poets to continental European collections, suggests a deliberate thematic or chronological layering in the curation process. The presence of works from various colonies and later nations further emphasizes the global ambition of the compilation, acknowledging the complex relationship between imperial literary traditions and emerging national voices.

Franz von Bodmann was the camp's surgeon. Altogether only 15 Germans served in the camp, most of the guards were provided by Estonian and Russian auxiliaries of the 287th and 290th Security Battalions (Schutzmannschaftsbataillone). The camp was established in the beginning of August 1943 near the Vaivara train station. It served as the main camp (Hauptlager) of 20 forced labor camps located throughout Estonia, some of which existed for brief times, and all together being commonly referred to as the Vaivara camp complex. At first the camp was run by the OT, but after a few weeks Kurt Pannicke took over. When Pannicke took over the Narva subcamp at the end of September, Helmut Schnabel became commander. In autumn 1944, some of the inmates were evacuated by sea to the Stutthof concentration camp. From there they were distributed to the satellite camps of Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp. Conditions and prisoners Since the main purpose of the camps was the fullest exploitation of the work capacity of their inmates, no large-scale killings of the able-bodied took place in the camps. Prisoners in the concentration camp had to work in the nearby forest, a quarry, or in the oil shale extraction. Those prisoners too old or too sick to work were killed in Selektionen (selections), as were children. The first such selection took place in the autumn of 1943, when 150 Jewish men and women were shot in the nearby woods. A second selection involved 300 Jews, most of them suffering from typhoid fever. In twenty more selections, approximately 500 more Jewish prisoners were murdered, including a group of children. From Bodmann's reports, the camp population in the whole complex was 6,982 in October 1943, 9,207 in November 1943, 8,210 in February 1944 and 6,662 in June 1944. In December 1943, a typhoid epidemic broke out in the camps, resulting in the deaths of 20 per cent of the camp population. Evacuation With the front coming closer in early 1944, the Vaivara camp was evacuated on 4 and 5 February 1944. 2,466 inmates were marched to the camps at Kiviõli (), Ereda (), Jõhvi () and Goldfields (). The inmates had to walk for three days in bad winter weather with poor clothing, footwear and food. The columns were also attacked by Soviet aircraft. In July 1944, Bodmann held a strict selection, known as Ten Percent Selection, when one in ten of the inmates was selected and shot near Ereda. The forced labor assigned to the prisoners was arduous, involving backbreaking labor under extremely harsh environmental conditions. The work in the oil shale extraction pits was particularly brutal, demanding long hours in subterranean environments with inadequate ventilation. Malnutrition and disease were rampant throughout the complex, exacerbated by the meager rations provided to the inmate population. Medical records indicate that typhus, dysentery, and tuberculosis were among the most prevalent ailments. The authority figures maintained a policy of brutal discipline, with corporal punishment being a common method for enforcing labor quotas and obedience. The satellite camps, while operating under the umbrella of the Vaivara system, experienced variations in administration and severity of treatment. Some accounts suggest that conditions in the outlying camps were even more desperate than those at the main facility. The constant threat of arbitrary violence from the guards served as a pervasive psychological element of the captivity. Surviving prisoners often spoke of the systematic dehumanization process inherent in the camp structure, where individuality was stripped away in favor of productive capacity. The initial administrative setup by the OT transitioned into a more rigidly controlled, SS-influenced operation under Pannicke and subsequently Schnabel. The shift in command structure reflected the broader reorganization of the German occupation forces in the region as the war progressed. The evacuation in February 1944 was a chaotic affair, designed to temporarily remove the camp from immediate Soviet military proximity, but it merely shifted the suffering to other transit points. The subsequent "Ten Percent Selection" in July 1944 demonstrated that even as the military situation worsened, the exterminatory function of the camp system continued to operate with chilling efficiency.

It was anchored by the network's president and Chief Executive Officer, former Defense secretary and senator Orly Mercado and the News and Public Affairs department head Marigold Haber-Dunca. Because of Mercado's advocacy on being an environmentalist, the background are all adorned with plants On January 14, 2008, its late-night spin-off was aired as RPN NewsWatch Second Edition. The network's hourly news updates was renamed as NewsWatch Update until February 25, 2011. The show was reformatted into a reality show between June 7, 2008, and August 16, 2008. From the usual twice a day times of 5:30 pm and 11:00 pm, it became once a day at 5:30 pm and Reema Chanco was engaged as an additional anchor. RPN NewsCap replaced RPN NewsWatch Second Edition and started airing at midnight. In 2010, the timeslot was moved to 11:30 in the evening. Alongside RPN NewsCap, RPN NewsWatch started to air only on free TV on that date at 5 pm as ETC had occupied the RPN frequency on all cable providers nationwide. The shift to ETC necessitated adjustments in the news programming schedule. RPN NewsWatch began its broadcast at the traditional five o'clock time slot, exclusively on the terrestrial network signal. This transition marked a period of restructuring for the network's news presentation. The operational changes reflected the new corporate ownership and the evolving media landscape in the Philippines. The commitment to news delivery remained a core function, though the platforms and presentation formats underwent continuous modification. The network aimed to maintain its presence in the competitive television market while adapting to new partnerships and ownership structures. These changes impacted the on-air talent and the overall production quality of the news segments. The narrative surrounding the newscasts reflected the broader business maneuvers of the parent company. Prior to the ETC rebranding, the news division had shown flexibility, incorporating reality elements and targeting specific demographic segments through various spin-offs. This diversification was an attempt to capture a wider audience base beyond traditional news consumers. The continued evolution of its news broadcasts illustrates the dynamic nature of broadcast journalism in a rapidly changing media environment. Further changes in programming structure followed the consolidation of ETC's operations across different media platforms. The original ethos of environmental advocacy, symbolized by the initial set design, gradually gave way to the more commercially driven programming typical of the evolving corporate entity.

He was the chief executive of UkrAVTO since 1983, leading this once state-owned company through privatization and restructuring to a role of Ukraine's main automobile manufacturer, servicer and importer. Later Vasadze's business was diversified by entering the insurance market. His wealth was estimated in 2007 at being around US$ 780 million. But because car sales in Ukraine during 2009 fell by 72 percent his wealth was late 2010 estimated at US$230 million. Career Vasadze participates in Ukrainian politics, first as an advisor to Prime Minister Anatoliy Kinakh in 2002. Also in 2002 he was elected a member of the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) for For United Ukraine. Then he joined six factions and/or parliamentary groups: including the For United Ukraine faction, Labour Ukraine and Party of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs of Ukraine. His main and open political goal is to lobby the interests of automotive industry, particularly to protect and harmonize the business conditions for both the local manufacturers and the importers. In 2005 Vasadze became a member of Batkivschyna and thus part of the Yulia Tymoshenko Bloc (BYuT). During the 2006 and 2007 parliamentary elections, he was elected as a deputy to the Verkhovna Rada for this bloc. On December 2, 2010 Vasadze was excluded from the BYuT faction immediately after he voted for a new tax code as proposed by President Viktor Yanukovych. Early September 2011 Vasadze joined the Party of Regions faction. In 2012 he was re-elected into parliament on the party list of Party of Regions. On January 16, 2014 he voted for the laws that conflict with Constitution of Ukraine, Convention about the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, obligations and duties of Ukraine as a member of the UNO, CE and OSCE. In the 2014 Ukrainian parliamentary election Vasadze was placed 11th on the electoral list of Strong Ukraine. In the election Strong Ukraine failed to clear the 5% election threshold (it got 3.11% of the votes) thus Vasadze did not return to parliament. Tariel Vasadze has been long-time-owner of a private business-jet aircraft. In early 2008 he received a Bombardier Challenger 605, serial number 5725, which was initially operated by Execujet wearing the registration D-ACUA. His aviation interests have also included investment in other aerospace enterprises. The aircraft has been utilized for both private and business purposes throughout his ownership. Beyond his corporate and political endeavors, Vasadze has maintained a presence in public life through media appearances and industry forums. These platforms have served as avenues for him to articulate his views on economic policy and the trajectory of Ukraine's industrial sector. His involvement in various business associations underscores his dedication to the advancement of Ukrainian commerce. The relationship between his industrial holdings and his political activities has frequently been a subject of public and academic scrutiny, reflecting the complex interplay between oligarchic capital and governance in post-Soviet economies. His continued engagement in parliamentary life, despite electoral setbacks, demonstrates a persistent interest in shaping the legislative environment that affects his commercial interests. The automotive industry remains a central pillar of his public advocacy, where he consistently advocates for regulatory stability and market access for both domestic producers and foreign distributors. This focus reflects the strategic importance of the vehicle sector to the broader Ukrainian economy and to his own substantial business portfolio.

Campuses The main campus of the School of Medicine at UAB is located in Birmingham, not to be confused with the original University of Alabama campus located in Tuscaloosa, AL. The Huntsville campus was originally a part of the University of Alabama in Huntsville; however, in 1974 UAB assumed control over the Huntsville program. Montgomery UAB's Montgomery campus is a collaborative effort among UAB, Baptist Health and the city of Montgomery. Beginning in May 2014, 10 third-year medical students began taking classes in Montgomery. Basil Hirschowitz was the first to explore the stomach with his new invention, the fiber-optic endoscope, which is now in the Smithsonian Institution. UAB heart surgeon, the late John W. For his part, Richards recalled that John Paul and Talitha Getty "had the best and finest opium". Print designer Celia Birtwell, who married designer Ossie Clark, recalled Talitha Getty as one of a number of "beautiful people" who crossed her threshold in the late 1960s, while couturier Yves Saint Laurent likened the Gettys to the title of a 1922 novel by F Scott Fitzgerald as "beautiful and damned". By 1969, the dissolute lifestyle the Gettys were leading in Italy and Morocco had begun to wear on Talitha, who wished to pursue treatment for heroin and alcohol addiction and return to Britain. While the intoxicating allure of bohemian excess characterized much of their earlier public appearances, Talitha sought a respite from the excesses of international celebrity and substance use. The pressures of maintaining a highly visible and hedonistic lifestyle among the jet-set elite proved increasingly difficult to sustain for her. Her decision to seek help represented a turning point, signaling a move away from the perpetual state of glamorous, reckless abandon that had defined the Gettys' presence in the mid-to-late sixties. This period of introspection and recovery was not entirely free from drama, but it introduced a new dimension to the family dynamic, one focused on personal health alongside their ongoing social prominence. Despite these internal struggles, the Getty name continued to command attention in high society circles, albeit with a slightly altered narrative thread weaving through the tapestry of their public life. Their connections remained deep within the artistic and fashionable spheres, though perhaps with a more tempered engagement with the volatile energies that had previously characterized their associations.

In 1990, Cambrex was listed on the NYSE. Cambrex entered the pharmaceutical market in 1994 with the acquisition of Nobel Pharma Chemistry business, now known as Cambrex Karlskoga AB and Cambrex Profarmaco. Through multiple acquisitions during the late 1990s, the firm entered the bioscience and the chiral enzymatic catalyst markets. Cambrex acquired two contract biopharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in 2001, to bulk manufacture biologics and pharmaceutical ingredients from clinical to commercial scales. In 2007, the firm decided to focus on its core competencies and sold the biologics business to Lonza Group. In 2008, Prosyntest (now Cambrex Tallinn) was acquired, and Steve Klosk was appointed CEO, while remaining President. To broaden their biocatalysis platform, Cambrex acquired IEP in 2010, now known as Cambrex IEP. In 2013, Cambrex completed a major 7,000 sq. ft. facility expansion at Charles City, IA to increase API manufacturing capabilities for both existing products and a new product. Investment continued at Charles City, IA with a 45,000 sq. ft temperature and humidity-controlled cGMP warehouse space in 2015. Cambrex continued to invest in its sites in 2016. Charles City, IA saw a significant expansion of its cGMP API manufacturing and storage capabilities, while large-scale manufacturing capabilities in Karlskoga, Sweden increased with the installation of new multi-purpose reactors and control room upgrades. Additional investment in 2016 saw Cambrex open a new pilot plant at its site in Paullo (Milan) Italy, allowing greater speed and flexibility for small scale API production. In 2016, Cambrex also expanded in its clinical stage API capabilities with the acquisition of PharmaCore, Inc. in High Point, NC, a leading early phase chemistry specialist with expertise in developing, scaling up and manufacturing small molecule APIs for clinical phase projects. In 2017, Cambrex invested in new small scale capacity at its Charles City, IA facility with the installation of two 500 gallon glass lined reactors and created a third small scale work center, further increasing flexibility for customer projects. Additional investment in Charles City, IA was seen in the form of a new $24 million facility to manufacture highly potent APIs (HPAPIs). Cambrex also expanded its newly acquired High Point, NC facility with the addition of a new $3.2 million, 11,000 sq.ft. analytical laboratory, in response to growing customer demand for analytical development and validation services in support of cGMP products at the clinical stage. The company continued its strategic expansion in subsequent years, emphasizing the integration of advanced chemical and biological manufacturing processes. Cambrex maintained a strong focus on enhancing its capabilities across the entire drug development lifecycle, from early-stage clinical material supply to large-scale commercial production. The strategic positioning of its global manufacturing sites allowed it to service a diverse international clientele requiring highly specialized chemical synthesis and biological processing. This diversified operational footprint provided customers with the assurance of localized support while benefiting from world-class technological infrastructure at each facility. The emphasis on process chemistry and biocatalysis allowed Cambrex to offer innovative, sustainable synthetic routes for complex active pharmaceutical ingredients, reducing environmental impact while improving reaction efficiency. The company's commitment to regulatory compliance, evidenced by the consistent upgrades to its cGMP facilities, solidified its standing as a reliable partner in the highly scrutinized pharmaceutical industry. Furthermore, the expansion into highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients addressed a growing need within oncology and specialized therapeutics, which require stringent containment and handling protocols. It was during this tenure that he became known as one of the leading rabbis of Europe for his erudition and strict adherence to halakha. It was also during this time that Rabbi Chaim Michael Dov Weissmandl joined his yeshiva and formed a life-long attachment to him. In 1931, Ungar was approached by the town of Nitra, which had recently lost its chief rabbi, Rabbi Avraham Aharon Katz, with a request that he head that community. To sweeten the offer, the community promised to help him expand its yeshiva under his leadership. Weissmandl tried to dissuade Ungar from accepting the offer, arguing that it would be a mistake to leave an established community like Trnava for Nitra, which was only about 200 years old and had 3,000 Jews. Ungar, however, said he would go. "My heart tells me that the day will come when there will be no yeshiva anywhere in Slovakia but Nitra, and I want to be there when that happens", he said presciently. In Nitra, Ungar built up a yeshiva with nearly 300 students that eventually attracted students from Czechoslovakia, Romania, Austria, and Germany. He taught in the classic Hungarian style introduced by the Chasam Sofer, and although he did not set out to produce rabbis, some of his students did go on to become prominent rabbis in their hometowns. He developed a close and loving relationship with each student, and kept the connection after they left, conducting an alumni re-union every five years. Weissmandl married his Rav's daughter, Bracha Rachel, in 1937, and became Ungar's right-hand man in all aspects of running the yeshiva. Besides his position as the chief rabbi of Nitra, Ungar was appointed vice president of the Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, the supreme religious body of World Agudath Israel, in 1935. World War II Persecution of Jews began even before World War II in Slovakia, where the Munich Agreement of 1938 carved Czechoslovakia into separate states. Slovakia became a totalitarian state run by the Catholic priest Jozef Tiso, who allied with Nazi Germany and supported discrimination against his country's Jews. In 1942, deportations from Slovakia to Auschwitz, via Lublin, began. The first Jews were forced to leave Nitra on the Shabbat after Passover. The community of Nitra, like countless others throughout the region, suffered immense turmoil under the Nazi occupation and the oppressive regime of the Slovak State. Rabbi Ungar and his students faced escalating threats as the machinery of the Holocaust ground into full operation. The yeshiva, which had been a beacon of Jewish learning and community life, found itself increasingly besieged by external pressures and internal fear. The strict adherence to religious law that defined Ungar’s teaching style also provided a framework for moral resistance during a period demanding profound ethical choices. Despite the encroaching darkness, the intellectual and spiritual life nurtured within the walls of the institution remained a vital, albeit perilous, sanctuary for the Jewish people of the area. The efforts to maintain religious continuity became an act of defiance against the nihilism of the surrounding political forces. The personal impact of the persecution on Rabbi Weissmandl was equally profound; his commitment to Ungar translated into an unwavering devotion to preserving the traditions and integrity of the yeshiva even when material existence seemed impossible. As the deportations accelerated, the focus shifted from expanding the yeshiva’s reach to safeguarding the lives and souls of those within it. The communal structure, which Ungar had carefully cultivated, became the last line of defense against complete dissolution. Records indicate that many of the students, recognizing the impending danger, attempted to organize clandestine efforts to secure passage or to hide within the community structures, often guided by the wisdom imparted by their teacher. After the liberation of Slovakia, the aftermath presented a landscape of devastation, marked by profound demographic loss and the physical wreckage of established institutions. The continuity of the yeshiva, while miraculously preserved in spirit by the resilience of its survivors, required immense rebuilding efforts. Rabbi Ungar, though physically and emotionally scarred by the ordeal, continued to play a central role in the spiritual reconstitution of the shattered community. The survival of the teaching tradition, even amidst the destruction of physical infrastructure and the loss of countless members, became a testament to the enduring power of the religious commitment fostered under his guidance. This period marked a transition from a life of scholarly ascent to one of desperate communal survival and subsequent spiritual reclamation.

Some of the more frequently seen forms of PID include common variable immunodeficiency, severe combined immunodeficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, ataxia–telangiectasia, Treatment The treatment of primary immunodeficiencies depends foremost on the nature of the abnormality. Somatic treatment of primarily genetic defects is in its infancy. Most treatment is therefore passive and palliative, and falls into two modalities: managing infections and boosting the immune system. Reduction of exposure to pathogens may be recommended, and in many situations prophylactic antibiotics or antivirals may be advised. In the case of humoral immune deficiency, immunoglobulin replacement therapy in the form of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) may be available. Antibiotic prophylaxis is also commonly used to prevent respiratory tract infections in these patients. In cases of autoimmune disorders, immunosuppression therapies like corticosteroids may be prescribed. For primary immunodeficiencies that are caused by genetic mutation does not exist a causal therapy that would "repair" the mutation. Although there is a therapeutic option, gene therapy which has been in a trial for few immune deficiencies affecting the hematopoietic system. Over the past two decades there were some successful treatments of patients with specific primary immunodeficiencies (PID), including X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome and metabolic conditions such as leukodystrophy. Gene therapy evolved in the 90s from using of gammaretroviral vectors to more specific self-inactivating vector platforms around 2006. The viral vectors randomly insert their sequences into the genomes. However, it is rarely used because of a risk of developing post-treatment T-cell leukemia as a result of interfering tumor-suppressor genes and because of ethical issues. But the progress in gene therapy is promising for the future of treating primary immunodeficiencies. Epidemiology A survey of 10,000 American households revealed that the prevalence of diagnosed primary immunodeficiency approaches 1 in 1200. This figure does not take into account people with mild immune system defects who have not received a formal diagnosis. Milder forms of primary immunodeficiency, such as selective immunoglobulin A deficiency, are fairly common, with random groups of people (such as otherwise healthy blood donors) having a rate of 1:600. Other disorders are distinctly more uncommon, with incidences between 1:100,000 and 1:2,000,000 being reported. Research Bone marrow transplant may be possible for Severe Combined Immune Deficiency and other severe immunodeficiences. Virus-specific T-lymphocytes (VST) therapy is used for patients who have received hematopoietic stem cell transplantation that has proven to be unsuccessful. It is a treatment that has been effective in preventing and treating viral infections after HSCT. VST therapy uses active donor T-cells that are isolated from alloreactive T-cells which have proven immunity against one or more viruses. Immunological research continues to investigate novel approaches to managing these complex disorders. Understanding the precise molecular pathways disrupted in various PIDs is crucial for developing targeted interventions beyond broad-spectrum treatments. For example, research into B-cell function in agammaglobulinemia focuses on restoring proper antibody production, while studies in combined immunodeficiency aim to improve T-cell reconstitution. The development of monoclonal antibodies designed to target specific defective immune components represents a promising avenue for future therapeutic development. Furthermore, advances in high-throughput screening technologies allow researchers to identify previously unknown genes associated with immune dysregulation, potentially leading to the identification of entirely new classes of PIDs. Clinical trials are increasingly incorporating precision medicine concepts, tailoring treatment regimens based on the specific genotype of the patient rather than solely on the phenotypic presentation of the illness. The ethical considerations surrounding advanced biological interventions, particularly gene editing techniques like CRISPR-Cas9, remain a major focus of both the scientific community and regulatory bodies. These tools hold immense potential to correct pathogenic mutations directly within patient cells, offering a curative paradigm shift away from chronic management. Long-term follow-up studies on current therapies are essential to monitor for delayed adverse effects, such as secondary malignancies or the development of autoimmunity following intensive immune modulation. These comprehensive research efforts aim to move PID management from a state of palliative care toward definitive, curative solutions for affected individuals worldwide.

Other films by Bhandit include Classmates, which won best picture, best director and best screenplay in 1990; Miss You, winner of best picture, best director and best screenplay in 1993, and Once Upon a Time, the hit comedy film series Boonchoo. His drama, Kalla khrung nueng ... muea chao nee (Once Upon a Time ... This Morning), won awards for best director and best screenplay and was submitted as Thailand's Best Foreign Language Film for the 68th Academy Awards in 1995. The Moonhunter Bhandit became controversial in 2001 with the release of The Moonhunter (14 tula, songkram prachachon or 14 October: War of the People), a biographical film about 1970s Thammasat University student activist and communist rebel Seksan Prasertkul, who co-wrote the screenplay. The English title refers to an episode when Seksan was fighting in the jungles of Thailand and, one night, startled by the rise of the moon, he fired his rifle at it. The Censorship Board banned the film's trailer, which included stock footage from 14 October 1973 student uprising, with soldiers and policemen beating up unarmed pro-democracy demonstrators. Bhandit then vowed to not release the film if the board made any cuts, but the board responded that Bhandit was simply using the censorship review process as a means of generating publicity for his film. As it turned out, the film was released without any cuts, a sign, Bhandit said, that Thai society was maturing. The film was submitted by Thailand for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Subsequent films, the CGI-heavy The Tigress of King River, the science fiction film, Ukkabat (Meteor) and the swashbuckling period film, The Magnificent Five generated neither controversy nor critical acclaim. Despite health problems including diabetes and a heart attack, Bhandit continued to work. "What else I can do? Run a noodle shop?" the director was quoted as saying by The Nation in 2006. "I have to work. I don't have much time because a director of my age is going to be out of fashion soon." In 2008, he made a critical and commercial comeback with Boonchu 9, which revived his hit teen comedy series highlighting the clash of rural and urban cultures. This sequel reinvigorated his comedic formula, proving that his ability to engage with popular tastes remained intact even as his personal challenges mounted. His later works continued to explore themes of societal change and the friction between tradition and modernity, although often through a more commercially palatable lens than his earlier politically charged projects. The transition from the fiery activism evident in The Moonhunter to the lighthearted escapism of Boonchu 9 represented a pragmatic adaptation to the shifting landscape of the Thai film industry and his own evolving personal circumstances. Critics noted this shift, sometimes praising the successful revitalization of a beloved property, other times suggesting a dilution of his earlier artistic ambition. Nevertheless, Bhandit demonstrated a remarkable resilience, maintaining a prolific output throughout the 2000s. His commitment to filmmaking transcended the limitations imposed by his physical ailments or the volatile reception of his more controversial endeavors. He remained a figure capable of bridging high-art ambition with mass entertainment appeal, a characteristic that defined his diverse body of work. His enduring presence in the industry solidified his status not merely as a director, but as a cultural commentator whose films, regardless of their genre, reflected facets of contemporary Thai life.

These rūnanga function as the primary representative bodies for the constituent hapū within the iwi structure. Their responsibilities encompass cultural preservation, the maintenance of traditional protocols, and engagement with contemporary political and social spheres. The formal structure allows for the collective management of tribal assets and the representation of hapū interests in regional and national forums. Decisions made at the rūnanga level often influence community practices concerning land use, customary rights, and cultural revitalization initiatives. The transition to the Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Awa in 2005 marked a significant administrative shift, centralizing decision-making processes under a unified governance framework. This consolidation aimed to streamline advocacy and ensure consistent representation across the geographically diverse communities affiliated with Ngāti Awa. The scope of their authority extends to overseeing marae maintenance and supporting cultural education programs for younger generations. Furthermore, they facilitate the relationship between the iwi and external governmental bodies, navigating legislative frameworks pertaining to Māori customary law and land tenure. The operational effectiveness of the rūnanga is closely tied to the active participation of its hapū members, ensuring that governance remains rooted in the needs and traditions of the people.

Nevertheless, the Commonwealth introduced a uniform income tax through an intricate scheme of four pieces of legislation. The Income Tax Act 1942, raised income tax levels to the existing state levels, setting it at such a rate that made it politically impossible for states to impose their own income taxes. The amount raised was enough to cover the war effort and grants for the states The States Grants Act 1942, provided a grant for each state equal to what it would have raised on its own income tax, on the condition that it did not raise its own income tax Section 221 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1942, required taxpayers to meet their Commonwealth tax liabilities before state tax liabilities the Income Tax (Wartime Arrangements) Act 1942, required that the states transfer to the Commonwealth all state staff, offices, furniture and records used to collect income tax The laws were challenged by the states of South Australia, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia. Decision The High Court held the laws were valid, despite the practical result being the inability of the states to impose income tax. The Income Tax Act 1942, was held to be valid despite the fact the rate was so high as to preclude the states from imposing income tax. As taxation is a non-purposive power, regardless of the object of the law, the subject matter was taxation, and hence valid under section 51(ii) of the Constitution. The States Grants Act 1942, was held to be valid, despite its coercive effect. The Commonwealth can use the section 96 grants power to induce a state to exercise its own powers as well as abstain from using its powers. Hence the Commonwealth can do such things to encourage or discourage a state from exercising its powers, which are technically not coercion. While the Act made it almost impossible for the States to continue taxing, Chief Justice John Latham noted that the states still had the choice not to accept Commonwealth grants. Justice Edward McTiernan also considered the Act valid under the defence power. Section 221 of the Income Assessment Act 1942, was held to be valid pursuant to section 51(ii) or was at the least valid under the implied incidental power. The subject matter of the law and the purpose of the law were both with respect to matters of taxation. McTiernan justified this section as valid under the defence power. The Income Tax (Wartime Arrangements) Act 1942, was upheld by a majority under the defence power. Aftermath The decision in relation to section 221 of the Income Assessment Act 1942 was subsequently overturned by the High Court in the Second Uniform Tax case. The High Court's affirmation of Commonwealth fiscal dominance during the war period established a significant precedent regarding the limits of state taxing power when confronted by national emergencies. This judicial endorsement underscored the federal structure's capacity for national uniformity, particularly when the matter in question related directly to revenue generation necessary for wartime prosecution. The reliance on the defence power to justify the legislation represented a powerful constitutional assertion by the Commonwealth government, effectively subordinating state financial autonomy to the exigencies of national defence. Although the initial rulings provided the necessary legal backing for the wartime financial restructuring, the subsequent review concerning Section 221 highlighted the judiciary's ultimate capacity to refine or overturn earlier interpretations of constitutional boundaries. The shift in legal understanding concerning the scope of the defence power and the nature of taxation powers continued to be a point of contention in Australian constitutional jurisprudence for decades following the conflict. This period of centralized fiscal control provided a practical demonstration of the Commonwealth's operational capacity, even if its constitutional justification was subject to later judicial scrutiny and refinement. The establishment of a national tax baseline, however, proved to be a lasting structural change in Australian financial administration.

(1987): Schmetterlinge in Berlin-West. These publications reflect a growing scientific interest in entomology and ornithology during the latter half of the eighteenth century. The systematic cataloging and detailed description of local fauna, particularly moths and nocturnal birds, were common pursuits among naturalists of the era. The emphasis on local occurrences, such as the fauna of the Berlin region, suggests an engagement with regional natural history surveys, which were important complements to the broader Linnaean classifications. The inclusion of specific species names, such as Sphinges Linnaei and Noctuas, indicates the authors were working within the established binomial nomenclature system developed by Carl Linnaeus. The focus on specific life stages, such as the caterpillars (Raupen) and the resulting moths (Phalæna), highlights an early recognition of the metamorphic cycles within insect life. Furthermore, the treatise addressing the methods for destroying harmful caterpillars points to a practical, applied aspect of natural history, addressing agricultural concerns prevalent in agrarian societies. The consistent serialization across issues of the Berlinisches Magazin suggests a commitment to a sustained, methodical presentation of findings rather than isolated essays. The references provided at the conclusion further contextualize the material, indicating that this work was situated within a wider body of regional historical and biological documentation. The study of night-flying insects, in particular, attracted considerable attention due to their often elusive nature and striking appearances, exemplified by the detailed descriptions of rare specimens like Phalaena pyritoides. These descriptions served not only as scientific records but also as contributions to the burgeoning field of amateur and professional natural history literature.

He later participated to the Tour de Luxembourg to fine-tune his form before the Tour de France, amassing 2 stage wins in the process. On the last stage, Greipel soloed to the finish line, a rare feat for such a pure sprinter. Right before the Tour, Greipel added another win to his tally at the Ster ZLM Toer. At the Tour, success came on the sixth stage in Reims after rival fast men Arnaud Démare and Marcel Kittel had been dropped from the peloton. Greipel outsprinted Alexander Kristoff () and Samuel Dumoulin () to claim the first step of the podium. 2015 Greipel took his first victory of the season at the Volta ao Algarve. He then waited until the second stage of Paris–Nice to grab the next one, dedicating the victory to his mother, who he said "is going through a very hard time". In April, he was denied his third victory of the season as he was edged by 3/10,000th of a second on the finish line by Alexander Kristoff at the Three Days of De Panne. At the end of the month, he renewed with victory on the fourth stage of the Tour of Turkey. As some of his main rivals were dropped on a climb close to the finish, he won the sprint of the reduced group. His next victory was Stage 6 of the Giro d'Italia ahead of Matteo Pelucchi and Sacha Modolo. He then withdrew from the Giro ahead of stage 14. He grabbed his next success on Stage 1 of the Tour de Luxembourg. At the Tour de France, Greipel was the victor of the second stage, a very windy affair that saw splits occur in the peloton. He was in the front group and out-sprinted Peter Sagan, Mark Cavendish and Fabian Cancellara. On the fifth stage, a bunch sprint occurred and Greipel got the better of it by besting Sagan and Cavendish. He also won the bunch sprints at the end of stages 15 in Valence and the final stage (stage 21) to Paris on the Champs-Élysées, giving him four stage victories — the most of any competitor at that year's Tour de France. 2016 Greipel took three sprint victories on the Giro d'Italia before deciding to withdraw before the mountains. His performance in the Tour de France cemented his status as a major contender in the sprinting discipline at the highest level of professional cycling. The consistency displayed across multiple Grand Tours highlighted his adaptability to different race conditions and terrain. In subsequent years, his focus continued to be on major stage races, though the competitive landscape of sprinting evolved significantly. Other sprinters began to challenge his dominance, often employing more tactical approaches or possessing superior endurance capabilities to sustain high speeds over longer distances. Greipel continued to participate in numerous UCI World Tour events throughout his career, seeking opportunities to showcase his raw sprinting power. His victories often came from the fast, decisive stages, where the peloton was either broken up by crosswinds or reduced to a small, manageable group before the final kilometers. Despite the increasing global competition, his capacity to deliver wins in high-pressure scenarios remained a notable aspect of his career narrative. He maintained a high profile in European cycling circuits, often featuring in prestigious one-day races as well as multi-stage events. The technical demands of modern cycling, particularly the increased use of aerodynamics and power output from modern equipment, presented a continuous challenge to sprinters accustomed to the power levels of previous generations. His enduring presence in these demanding races serves as a testament to his commitment and physical conditioning throughout his tenure as a professional athlete.

Truet was a Tour member who was killed in a car accident during the 2006 season. The award was renamed in her honor beginning in 2006. It is named in honor of the Tour's founder and former president, Eloise Trainor. The Futures Tour served as a vital developmental circuit for aspiring professional golfers seeking entry into the elite ranks of the LPGA. Competitors on this tour often exhibited a high degree of tenacity, as the competition provided a proving ground under demanding conditions. Success on the Futures Tour frequently paved the way for invitations to major LPGA events or provided the necessary ranking points for direct entry into the main tour. The structure of the tour allowed players to gain valuable competitive experience against a wide array of international talent, fostering a diverse and challenging playing field. Participation in televised events such as The Big Break offered these golfers increased visibility, providing exposure that could attract sponsors and further career opportunities. Beyond the specific contestants featured in the mentioned broadcasts, the Futures Tour continually cycled through emerging talent, representing various collegiate programs and international golf systems. The rigorous travel schedule and the constant pressure to perform in a lower-tier, yet highly competitive, environment shaped the professional demeanor of those who persevered. The progression from the Futures Tour to the LPGA circuit was not always linear, involving periods of striving, re-entry, and continuous self-improvement.

These distinct municipal boundaries reflect the complex administrative evolution of the Auckland region over the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. Prior to significant local government reforms, these areas operated under various local authorities, often with overlapping or shifting jurisdictions. The amalgamation of numerous smaller entities into the current unitary council structure necessitated the careful consolidation of services, assets, and civic identities across vastly different demographic and geographic profiles. The North Shore, for instance, retained a strong, distinct character even after integration, characterized by affluent residential pockets interspersed with more commercially oriented zones. Similarly, the eastern suburbs developed their own unique socioeconomic stratification, contrasting the established, historic areas near the harbor with newer developments further inland. The former Manukau City area presents a particularly diverse tapestry, encompassing both older, established working-class communities and rapidly developing peripheral zones experiencing significant population influx. The Papakura District, situated further south, maintained a more distinctly suburban and semi-rural feel, which influenced its planning and infrastructure development patterns separately from the more densely urbanized central areas. The differing historical contexts of these former local bodies—some rooted in agricultural settlement, others in maritime trade or industrial growth—are visible in the present-day urban fabric and the specific needs of the populations residing within these named localities. Contemporary urban planning in Auckland must therefore navigate these layered histories, attempting to forge a cohesive regional identity while respecting the ingrained local characteristics of each suburb and district. Transportation networks, utility provision, and public safety strategies are now managed across these former boundaries, presenting ongoing logistical challenges for regional governance. The sheer diversity represented by this list, ranging from high-density inner-city nodes like Ponsonby to more sprawling, less dense areas such as parts of South Auckland, underscores the multifaceted nature of modern Auckland.
